fix(desktop): report and mute a Browser guest that attaches after its session is hidden

The off-screen hook only re-ran when hidden/parked changed, and a guest has
no webContents id until it attaches. A page whose session was parked between
mount and attach was never reported hidden to main (so mouse back/reload
could still target it) and never muted. The pane now feeds the guest's
dom-ready to the hook, which re-reports and re-mutes for the attached id.

refactor(desktop): move preview tab ownership into store/preview-ownership.ts

preview.ts had grown to ~1450 lines. Who-owns-this-tab logic — compression
rotation aliases, the pending-runtime map, owner identity, ownsTab /
bucketTabsFor, the drawer visibility predicate — now lives in a topical
sibling. preview.ts keeps the tab list, its per-profile storage and the bucket
writers (adopt/rekey/prune), which need that storage. bucketTabsFor takes the
viewed bucket as a parameter instead of reading preview.ts's module state, so
the sibling has no import cycle back into preview.ts.

Behaviour-identical: importers of PreviewOwner and forgetPendingRuntimeTabs
now import from preview-ownership (no re-export shim).

test(desktop): prove the kept Browser body survives A -> B -> A, not the registration identity

The keep-alive test compared the pane registration object across a session
switch — an implementation detail. It now renders the layout tree and asserts
what the user gets: A's body element stays connected (hidden, inert) while B
is shown, is the same node with the same input value when A returns, mounted
once and never disconnected. Red on the pre-keep-alive head f5f54a2b6c9.

fix(desktop): mute a hidden session's kept Browser and restore its sound on return

A hidden session's live Browser stays mounted so returning shows the same
page, but it kept playing audio into the chat the user had switched to. The
parked-pane set is now an atom; a preview pane whose tab is parked mutes its
guest (webview.setAudioMuted) and unmutes on return only if it was the one that
muted it, so a page muted beforehand stays muted. Inactive tabs in the session
on screen keep playing, like background tabs in a browser.

Timers/rendering: a CSS-hidden webview still reports visible to Chromium and
Electron has no public API to mark a guest hidden without detaching it (any
detach destroys the guest, losing its state), so throttling is left as is.

fix(desktop): mouse back/forward and reload never act on a hidden session's Browser

After a session switch, Chromium still tracked the hidden session's kept
Browser guest as the focused webContents, so main's focused-guest gestures
(mouse back/forward app-command, swipe, Ctrl/Cmd+R) navigated or reloaded a
page the user could not see. The keep-alive host also left focus on an inert
hidden guest, where keystrokes could still land.

- A keep-alive host going hidden blurs whatever inside it holds focus.
- The preview pane tells main when its guest leaves / returns to the screen
  (hermes:preview-guest-hidden; only the embedding renderer is believed), and
  commandFocusedGuest (moved to electron/preview-guest-offscreen.ts) skips a
  hidden guest so the gesture falls through to the renderer's visible pane.

fix(desktop): a fresh draft's drawer no longer shows another runtime's pending tab

tabVisibleTo matched every ownerless tab when no session was focused, so a
runtime's pending tab (opened before its stored id bound) leaked into a fresh
draft's drawer and into any other runtime's. A pending tab is now visible only
while its own runtime is the one on screen; a true draft tab (no runtime) stays
in the draft.

fix(desktop): keep a hidden session's live Browser mounted across session switches

Switching A -> B -> A unmounted A's Browser (its pane contribution was
disposed), so returning made a new Electron guest: unsaved input and page
JS state were lost, where main kept them. A preview tab whose session leaves
the screen now leaves the layout tree but keeps its contribution, so its
keep-alive host stays mounted (hidden, inert, aria-hidden, no pointer
events) and the same guest re-docks on return. Parked panes are excluded
from tree adoption (parked-panes.ts). Retention is capped at 8 hidden live
pages, longest-hidden first; past the cap a page unmounts and reloads from
its saved row when its session returns. Agent tools are unaffected: they
resolve tabs by owner, never by what is mounted.

fix(desktop): agent preview tools see only their own profile's pins and runtime's tabs

Two ownership holes in the per-session preview scoping:

- Cross-profile pins (P1): previewTabsFor read the viewed profile's bucket
  and admitted its pins unconditionally, and previewTabIdsVisibleTo
  authorized them for the pop-out bridge, so profile X's tile could
  preview.read profile Y's pinned page. The requester's owner now carries
  the profile its runtime belongs to (previewScopeForRuntime, the same
  resolution the rail scope uses); pins count only in that profile's
  bucket, own tabs count wherever they live. Agent opens and closes use the
  same identity, so X can neither navigate nor close Y's pinned Browser.

- Pending-runtime pool (P2): an ownerless tab was visible to every requester
  with no stored id, so runtime B read, reused (navigated) and closed runtime
  A's pre-stored-id Browser. Ownerless tabs are now either a runtime's pending
  tab (that runtime only) or a true draft tab (the draft on screen only:
  the primary's runtime, or a request naming no runtime) across reads,
  reuse and closes.

Human UI paths ($visiblePreviewTabs, the focused drawer) are unchanged.

fix(desktop): deleting a session prunes its preview tabs in every profile bucket

prunePreviewTabsForSession only filtered the viewed profile's tabs, so
deleting profile X's session while Y was on screen left X's unpinned tabs in
X's bucket and in storage. Prune every bucket (pins survive) and persist.

fix(desktop): preview tab menu reads the live pin state so Pin toggles back to Unpin

The zone menu's pin row captured `pinned` when the pane registered, and the
mirror keeps a same-title registration for the tab's whole life, so after the
first Pin the row kept offering Pin and kept setting true. Read the flag when
the menu renders and again on select.

fix(desktop): third-review follow-ups for per-session preview tabs

- A popped-out Browser now answers a background session in another
  profile: previewTabIdsVisibleTo reads every profile bucket, not only the
  one in view. A background bucket counts only when the requester has a tab
  of its own there, so one profile's pins never answer for another
  profile's session.
- Agent preview tools act for the requesting runtime as well as its stored
  id (PreviewOwner): a tab that runtime opened before its stored id bound
  stays drivable/readable once the selection already names that id, locally
  and through the pop-out bridge.
- A runtime whose session state is dropped before it binds a stored id
  drops its pending notes (dropSessionState / clearAllSessionStates), so
  the next draft's first send adopts those tabs instead of skipping them.
- The drawer's pending-tab clause skips a LISTED selection: a cold resume
  selects an existing session a beat before it unbinds the old runtime, and
  that runtime's pending tab no longer joins the resumed drawer. An unlisted
  id (the runtime's own stored id arriving) still shows it.
- server-requests.test pop-out mocks forward the owner and assert it.

test(desktop): statusbar test mock exposes $focusedSessionIsTile

The preview store now derives visible tabs from session-focus's
$focusedSessionIsTile; the statusbar test's session-focus mock lacked it,
so the suite failed at import.

fix(desktop): scope every agent preview tool to the requesting session

Second-pass review of the per-session preview tabs:

- drive_preview, tour, nav, input and the script runner resolve the
  requester's tab (storedSessionIdForRuntimeId of the event's runtime) via
  the shared resolveActivePreviewTab, not the focused session's; an id that
  does not resolve reads the ownerless/draft view, never the focused one.
- Pre-stored-id agent tabs are handed over when THAT runtime's stored id
  binds (handleTransition / ensureSessionState), and openPreview stamps the
  event's runtime rather than whichever runtime is active.
- Requests forwarded to a popped-out Browser carry the requester's tab ids;
  a pop-out showing another session's tab stays silent.
- Runtime notes are dropped with their tabs (close, prune, profile drop) and
  draft adoption skips tabs pending for a live runtime.
- The rotation-alias walk is bounded by the map size.

fix(desktop): hand a pre-stored-id agent preview to the runtime that opened it

With focus-driven adoption gone (F1), main's "keeps the tab when the
stored session id arrives afterwards" regressed: an agent's open_preview
right after a first send lands before the stored id, so the tab was
ownerless and vanished from the drawer once the id arrived.

openPreview now notes the runtime an ownerless tab was opened under
(memory-only; a fresh draft has no runtime, so its file-browser / "+"
Browser tabs carry no note). The tab is adopted only when THAT runtime's
stored id arrives, never when another session or tile takes the screen.

refactor(desktop): import the focused-session atoms from session-focus, drop the re-export shim

$focusedStoredSessionId / $focusedSessionIsTile moved to session-focus.ts
(to break the session-states <-> preview load cycle) but session-states
kept re-exporting them for its old importers - an internal-move compat
shim (independent review F5). Every importer now reads
'@/store/session-focus' and the re-export is gone.

Test plumbing follows the symbol: suites that stubbed the atom on the
session-states mock now stub it on session-focus (profile-routing) or use
the real derivation (open-session-refresh-in-place), and two
session-states assertions read the atom from the module that defines it.
session-sidebar-focus loads session-states for the primary-follow wiring
its last case asserts, as its old import did implicitly.

Also drops the dead $focusedStoredSessionId stub this PR had added to the
close-tab.test.ts mock (F8); the file is back to main.

fix(desktop): keep the agent's read_preview / drive_preview inside the session's tabs

resolveActivePreviewTab / readActivePreview, activePreviewInput and
activePreviewNav still read every session's tabs. With no visible
selection the tabs[0] fallback handed read_preview another session's
hidden tab, and the multi-tab meta listed hidden tabs' labels and URLs to
the model (independent review F3).

They now read previewTabsFor(session): the tabs that session can see (its
own plus pins). read_preview passes the requesting session's stored id;
drive_preview (active session only) uses the focused one. A popped-out
Browser renderer holds only its own tab, so it keeps reading that.

fix(desktop): resolve preview tab owners through compression rotation; one write per agent close

Independent review F2/F4/F9 on the session-scoped preview rail:

- F2 (hang): rekey(A,B) then a replayed rekey(B,A) put a cycle in the
  memory-only alias map and the latestSessionId walk spun forever, freezing
  $visiblePreviewTabs. Both ends of a rekey now resolve to their current
  tips first and a rekey that resolves to the same tip is ignored, so the
  map only ever links one tip to a different tip and stays acyclic.
- F4: a tab opened in the window between a rotation and focus following it
  was stamped with the rotated-away id; the alias map does not survive a
  relaunch, so the tab was orphaned. Opens, the strip "+" Browser and an
  unpin now stamp the resolved tip, and a deleted conversation is pruned by
  any of its ids.
- F9: close_preview with no url called closeRightRailTab per tab (N tab-list
  writes, N persists, N selection fix-ups). It now closes the session's
  unpinned tabs in one write and re-homes the selection once.

fix(desktop): keep a draft's preview tabs in the draft until its first send

A fresh draft has no stored id, so the tabs it opens are ownerless. The
focus listener adopted every ownerless tab on ANY null -> id focus change,
so a side tile taking focus, or an existing session clicked in the
sidebar, swallowed the draft's file / Browser tabs and the draft's drawer
came back empty (independent review F1, same symptom as M1).

Adoption is now an explicit call made where the draft's first send
assigns its stored id, beside the composer draft's own hand-over
(announceNewSessionDraftKey). Focus changes never re-own a tab.

fix(desktop): keep session-scoped preview tabs owned, restorable and rotation-safe

The session-scoped rail (#73890) regressed core preview flows and was
reverted in #130852. This keeps the scoping and fixes each regression:

- Ownership is explicit. The strip "+" Browser is stamped with the focused
  session, so it is visible at once and never adopted by another session
  on the next switch. openPreview takes an owner (default: the focused
  session); an agent preview.open/preview.close maps the event's runtime id
  to its stored id, so a side tile's agent previews land in, and close
  from, that tile's own drawer.
- Reuse is decided among the tabs the owner can see (its own plus pins):
  a URL open in session B never navigates session A's Browser, and an
  agent close without a url closes only that session's own tabs — never
  other sessions' tabs or pins.
- File tab ids are identity only. Lookups match a file by canonical path
  among the owner's visible tabs, so ids never need rekeying: ownerless
  tabs keep main's `file:<url>` id, owned ones `file:<owner>:<url>`.
  Restore keeps every row verbatim (the url dedupe that collapsed every
  Browser into one is gone), so pop-out finds a non-last Browser by id.
- Auto-compression tip rotation rekeys the conversation's tabs onto the
  new tip at both rotation sites (handleTransition and the state cache),
  and the old id stays an alias, so the tabs never blink out between the
  rotation and the focus following it.
- markPreviewTabMissing resolves by tab id or the file's url/path, which
  is what the file pane passes; the restored tombstone test is main's.
- Each session remembers the tab it had in front; switching back fronts
  it. Boot validates the persisted selection against every tab, not the
  (still unfocused) visible set.

The session-focus module's new imports broke tests whose vi.mock factories

fix(desktop): harden preview session-scoping reuse paths

Review feedback on #87288 (Enough1122 + cross-vendor validation):

- openPreview: reusing a pinned file row from another session keeps the
  owner's id (no id/sessionId split); the singleton Browser and artifacts

fix(desktop): scope preview tabs to the session that opened them

Preview tabs were window-global: a file/URL/artifact opened in one
conversation stayed visible above the composer in every other
conversation — including duplicates of the same file (file targets were
keyed by the raw URL, so file:// and plain-path entry points stacked).

Per the design proposed on #73890, tabs now belong to the session that
opened them (sessionId stamped at open), and the drawer renders only the
active session's tabs plus an explicit pinned set:

- pinned tabs render in every session (the deliberate cross-session
  workspace); a pin toggle rides on each preview tab's strip glyphs
- file tab ids are canonicalized (file:// stripped) so the same file
  dedupes across entry points; restored legacy rows are rekeyed and
  deduped on decode
- deleting a session drops its tabs (pins survive)
- legacy unscoped tabs migrate to pinned on load; ownerless tabs opened
  on a fresh draft are adopted into the session when one appears
- the terminal pane is untouched (process state stays global)

Tests: store unit tests for stamping/visibility/pin/prune/adoption/
canonicalization/migration, plus a mirror integration test proving the
drawer swaps panes on session switch. Full UI suite 561 files / 5529
tests green; typecheck and lint clean.

Partially addresses #73890 (the preview-tab scoping gap; the Artifacts

fix(tests): kanban wake drain helpers no longer busy-spin forever on Python 3.12+

tests/gateway/test_kanban_wake_acceptance.py intermittently hung until the
CI runner SIGKILLed it at 600s (normally ~4s). The faulthandler stack of a
reproduced hang is the loop thread inside the test's own drain() helper:

    while adapter._background_tasks:
        await asyncio.gather(*list(adapter._background_tasks))

Since Python 3.12, asyncio.gather() completes eagerly when every child is
already done, so `await gather(...)` returns without yielding to the event
loop. When a session task finishes in the same loop iteration that resumes
the test (e.g. right after the notifier's advance() to_thread hop), the task
is done but its _background_tasks.discard done-callback is still queued for
the next iteration. drain() then re-checks a set that can never shrink and
spins forever without ever letting the loop run that callback.

Yield once after each gather so queued done-callbacks run before the set is
re-checked. Same fix for the identical helper in
tests/gateway/test_completion_admission.py and evals/heartbeat_idle_wire.py.
Production code is not affected (BasePlatformAdapter.cancel_background_tasks
filters done tasks and is bounded to 5 rounds).

fix(dashboard): bound the PTY helper grace and await background closes

- Cap the helper grace at 2.0 s (and ignore non-finite or <= 0 env
  values) and wait only 0.5 s after SIGKILL, so a raised
  HERMES_TUI_GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_S cannot push close_all() past the
  backend SIGTERM -> SIGKILL budget.
- close_all() also awaits closes already running in the background
  (dead remnants, capacity evictions); the registry now holds those
  tasks, which also keeps them from being garbage-collected.
- _discard_output sleeps on EOF instead of spinning on a readable dead
  master, and catches ValueError from select() like read() does.

fix(dashboard): keep PTY teardown inside the shutdown budget and the save grace

- close_all() closed sessions one after another; each close may now
  wait out its helpers' SIGHUP grace, so N sessions could exceed the
  backend's SIGTERM -> SIGKILL budget (dashboard_procs) and strand the
  rest (#111912). Close them concurrently.
- attach_or_spawn awaited a dead remnant's close() under the
  registry-wide attach lock, stalling every new chat for the helper
  grace. Close it in the background, as capacity eviction already does.
- The helper grace now follows HERMES_TUI_GATEWAY_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_S
  (+0.5 s, at least 1.5 s), so a raised gateway grace is not cut short.
- close() drains the PTY master while it waits. The drain task has
  stopped reading by then, and on macOS an exiting child stays in exit
  until its pending terminal output is read: the leader was not reaped
  within 0.5 s, the loop escalated to SIGTERM on the whole group, and the
  gateway's SIGHUP save was killed mid-way.

fix(dashboard): end a PTY session's helpers after its leader dies

close() signalled the process group only while the PTY leader was
still alive, and read the group id from the leader at close time. When
the leader dies first (crash, OOM kill), or exits on SIGHUP while a
helper ignores it, the helpers keep the PTY slave open: no EOF arrives,
and after the reaper frees the slot nothing ever signals them, so they
and their memory outlive the session (#76759).

Record the group id at spawn. After the leader is gone:
- if the group was already sent SIGHUP while the leader lived, only wait
  up to 1.5 s for it, then SIGKILL. The TUI gateway in that group saves
  its sessions on SIGHUP within a 1.0 s grace (tui_gateway/entry.py);
  a second SIGHUP or an earlier SIGKILL would cut that save short;
- if the leader was already dead, send SIGHUP, wait, then SIGKILL.
Stop at ESRCH. The id cannot be reused while any member is alive.

Also drop the duck-typed _bridge_alive helper: PtyBridge.is_alive()
already catches its own errors, and the keepalive test fake now
implements is_alive() like the real bridge.

fix(dashboard): reap PTY sessions whose child process died without EOF (#76759)

reap_idle only freed a keep-alive PTY session on EOF (alive=False) or after
the detached TTL. If the child is killed while a grandchild still holds the
PTY slave, or the drain task dies, EOF never arrives and the dead TUI keeps
its registry slot, fds and memory forever. Also probe the bridge's
is_alive() (WNOHANG waitpid) in reap_idle.

fix(logging): keep records of a live profile whose logs/ was removed

When logs/ disappears but the profile itself is live (removed by hand,
no tombstone), the handler skipped the write and the router only
re-routed after a confirmed delete, so every record was silently dropped
until restart. Before the skip they were lost too, but loudly. Send a
skipped record to the default log whether or not the home is released.

fix(logging): flag a skipped write instead of reading it from a closed stream

The router re-routed a record when its handler's stream was None after
the write. On Windows concurrent-log-handler closes the stream after
every write, so every live-profile record read as skipped: the liveness
check ran per record (defeating the 2 s rate limit), the handler paid an
isdir() per emit, and a tombstoned home whose dir still existed got the
same record written twice (profile log, then default log).

The handler now sets skipped_missing_dir only when it actually skips
because logs/ is gone, and checks the directory only when the file is
missing or its reopen just failed. The rate-limit test also runs with a
handler that closes its stream after each write.

perf(logging): check a routed profile's liveness at most every 2 s

The out-of-band delete check added in the previous commit runs is_dir()
plus named_profile_is_deleted() on every record for a live named profile,
in every router: a live-profile emit went from 5 to 9 stat calls. Record
the last check per home and re-check only once _PROFILE_LIVENESS_RECHECK_S
(2.0 s) has passed. The first record seen for a home always checks, so a
home deleted before it ever logged is caught at once. The default home
still pays nothing.

An rmtree inside the interval must not bring back the FileNotFoundError
traceback from #103777. A routed per-profile handler that cannot reopen
because its logs/ directory is gone now skips the write. The router sees
the dropped stream, re-checks right away, releases the home and sends
that same record to the default log. A tombstone with the directory still
in place is noticed at the next interval check.

Scope: the stale fd for the deleted home is closed on the next routed
record after the tombstone or rmtree. This does not fix the Windows
rmtree failure. A CLI delete racing a live server's open handlers still
depends on release_profile_log_handlers in-process and on #130285.

Tests: the rmtree case no longer writes a tombstone first, so it covers
the missing-directory branch alone, inside the interval. The tombstone
case moves a patched _monotonic past the interval instead of sleeping. A
new test asserts one check per router for each interval.

fix(logging): release an out-of-band deleted profile from the log router

The fallback above stops records landing in a vanished profile home, but
it leaves two gaps for a CLI `hermes profile delete` behind a running
serve/dashboard:

- The routed handler for the deleted home is never closed. Its fd stays
  open on the unlinked agent.log (and, on Windows, the CLH lock files keep
  the rmtree failing), and every later record for that home pays the
  is_dir() stat again because the startup snapshot still names it.
- The CLI tombstones the profile before rmtree. Between the two steps the
  directory still exists, so records keep writing into a profile that is
  already deleted.

Treat either signal (missing dir or named_profile_is_deleted tombstone)
as a delete and call the existing release_profile() path the in-process
DELETE /api/profiles route already uses: it closes the handler and drops
the home from the routing set, so later records for it fall straight
through to the default home with no further checks. The default-home path
is unchanged (short-circuits before any stat).

fix(logging): route records to the default home when a profile is deleted

The profile-routing file handler keeps a static snapshot of the served
profile homes taken at startup. When 'hermes profile delete' removes a
home underneath a long-lived dashboard process, every record for that
home retries the vanished logs/ path: the managed rotating handler
stats, reopens, fails with FileNotFoundError and routes the error to
stderr — a repeating '--- Logging error ---' loop every logging tick
(#103777).

Fall back to the default home when a routed home's directory no longer
exists, mirroring the cron scheduler's _existing_profile_homes() filter.
The deleted profile's directory is never resurrected on disk and its
records keep flowing to the default home instead of being dropped with
stderr noise.

fix(tui): keep the observed parent for the Windows slash-worker watchdog

The spawn-time --parent-pid closes the POSIX startup race, but on Windows a
venv python.exe is a redirector that launches the base interpreter as its own
child, so the worker's direct parent is the launcher rather than the gateway.
Arming the getppid() watchdog on the gateway PID there would make it see a
mismatch on its first poll and os._exit() a healthy worker. Windows never
reparents anyway, so keep the observed PPID there (main's behaviour) and use
the spawn PID only on POSIX.

PID reuse needs no create-time pairing: the watchdog compares the kernel's
live getppid() against the recorded PID, and a process that later receives
that number never becomes this worker's parent.

ci: run the Python suite and the macOS lane as two slices each

The full suite was the last job to finish in 33 of 43 CI runs since it
moved from a 96-core to one 32-core runner (p50 666 s). That runner is
~90% packed, so only more machines help, and one bigger box is poor
value: on 96 cores the same files took 25-50% longer each and the suite
ran ~1.8x faster for 3x the price. Two 32-core slices scale linearly
(simulated from per-file CI timings: 262 s / 252 s vs 514 s on one box).

a newer cache between the two restores made timed LPT compute different
partitions per job, silently dropping or double-running files.

saves its own cache key on main; the runner keeps the restored entries

on #131236 and #131246). Skip the rerun when the head moved: the new run's

only when it predates the stamp (the #123314 leftover from a previous
install); one armed after it is retried as before. The shortcut also
requires a clean tree on both sides: a stamp recorded dirty, or local
edits since, are no proof that the built products match the checkout.

Reported by @unsupportedpastels in review.

refactor(desktop-update): keep only the reachable 124-after-completion remap

The Windows hand-off's idle watchdog is the only producer of exit 124 on
main (posix.sh has no watchdog and `hermes update` never exits 124), so
the posix remap was dead and goes. The retry-state helper and its
self-test arm collapse into one Resolve-HermesUpdateOutcome check, now
proved end to end through the real hand-off instead: a fake update that
prints its banner and parks silently past a 3 s ceiling surfaces as a
verified success with the gateway fleet restored.

The remap also refuses a run whose output already carries the
"Update not complete" verdict, which supersedes the banner.

fix(update): an adoption stamp never discharges an owed completion tail

Boot-time adoption of an unstamped blessed checkout publishes the same
identity a finished install/update does (commit == HEAD) but builds
nothing. Read as completion evidence, the launch that adopted (and every
later one) cleared a pending source-completion marker whose tail never
ran, and nothing on disk recorded the debt afterwards.

Adoption now stamps `adoptedAt`; the completed-tree check ignores such
stamps, and the next real completion rewrites the stamp without it. The
check also drops its blanket try/except: both reads it wraps never raise.

fix(desktop-update): completed update killed with exit 124 is terminal, never re-run (#96205)

Port of #96340 (Finn763) onto the current legacy-scoped retry gates,
narrowed to the watchdog sentinel only: exit 124 + the "Update complete!"
marker maps to success so the hand-off verifies and relaunches the new
build instead of re-running the completed update (the 70+ minute popup
retry storm). A plain exit 1 after the marker is the stale-gateway
verdict (hermes_cli/update_receipt.py) and must keep failing.

As first written this also added a posix.sh gate and a retry-state
helper with a -SelfTestRetryState arm; the next commit drops the posix
gate (nothing there exits 124) and replaces the helper and self-test
with one end-to-end test through the real hand-off.

Co-authored-by: Finn763 <165816600+Finn763@users.noreply.github.com>

fix(update): skip source-update completion when the stamp names HEAD

A fresh install records its tree in install-stamp.json; a first launch under a preserved or pristine home then re-entered the completion tail against the same SHA (stale pending marker, or no per-home facts). When the stamp commit is HEAD the products were already built for this tree: provision a stale venv without arming, discharge leftover markers, and run the agent. Fixes #123314.

fix(desktop): embed host answers malformed paths with 404 instead of throwing

`new URL("//", origin)` threw inside the http request handler, so a
request like `GET //` escaped as an uncaught main-process TypeError and
was never answered. Reject unparseable targets up front.

`hermes status --full` printed two lists for the same platforms: a legacy
table judged by one env var, then "(plugin)" rows judged by the gateway.
Slack configured in config.yaml showed "✗ not configured" and
"✓ configured (plugin)" in the same section, and the legacy verdict could

Render one list from the gateway config instead: registry entries bring

fix(gateway): skip cron runs in their own restart-safe scope in the restart wait

A cron run handed to an external worker in its own transient systemd scope
outlives the gateway: the shutdown drain deliberately leaves it unmarked
(``mark_running_jobs_interrupted``) and its final send rides the durable
delivery queue, drained by whichever gateway is live next. The after-turn
restart wait still counted it as active work, so ``/restart``, SIGUSR1 and
``hermes update`` held the gateway in ``draining`` — refusing every new turn —
for up to ``agent.restart_after_turn_timeout`` (30 min by default) while the
worker kept running regardless. Observed in the field: a 100-minute job turned
a restart into a ~30-minute lockout.

- ``cron.scheduler`` records whether an accepted handoff got its own scope
  (``dispatch.mode == "scoped"``) and exposes
  ``get_restart_safe_external_job_ids()``; runs already reported as wedged are
  excluded there too, because the gateway subtracts both counts and a run in
  both sets would be subtracted twice.
- ``_awaitable_work_count()`` subtracts that count as a second, disjoint
  exclusion; ``_describe_active_work()`` marks the unit (``restart_safe``).
- A degraded worker (external, but no reachable user bus, so it shares the
  gateway cgroup) is NOT listed and is still awaited — the restart would kill
  it mid-run.
- The wait and observation log lines now name both exclusion classes instead of
  claiming everything still listed will be interrupted.

Tests: tests/gateway/test_restart_drain.py (skip + control),
tests/cron/test_restart_safe_worker.py (registry contract).
Docs: updating.md restart section, cli-config.yaml.example.

fix(core): swap extension artifacts by copy when Windows locks the directory (#11889)

* fix(core): swap extension artifacts by copy when Windows locks the directory

Updating or uninstalling an extension failed on Windows with a bare
`EPERM: ... rename '~\.qwen\extensions\<name>' -> '...rollback\<uuid>'`, and
retrying could never fix it. The lock is Qwen's own: `ExtensionFileWatcher`
watches the extension tree with chokidar at unlimited depth, which attaches a
native change-notification handle to every subdirectory, and Windows refuses to
rename a directory whose descendant is open. The holder is usually a different
long-running session, so no single session can clear the way for the others.

The store now falls back to a copy-based swap for the whole transaction when
that rename fails with a lock error on Windows: back the installed tree up by
copying it under a provisional name and publish it with one rename, so a
half-copied backup can never be restored over an intact destination; copy the
staged tree over it; then prune the paths staging does not carry. Deleting and
copying are not blocked by those handles, which is what makes this workable
without any cross-process coordination. `rollbackJournal` learned the matching
direction, the strategy is recorded in the transaction journal, and journals
written by older builds keep their current recovery behaviour. When even the copy
cannot complete, the caller gets the directory and the reason instead of an
errno.

POSIX paths are unchanged: the fallback is gated on win32 and on a
lock-classified error. Releasing the acting session's own handles around a
mutation was tried and dropped - it only helps when that session is the sole
holder, and copy is reachable everywhere rename is. The design doc records that
and the non-atomicity the fallback accepts.

Verified with an isolated-HOME harness that holds the same handles a live session
holds: the released CLI fails both operations with EPERM, this build completes
both.

* fix(core): swap extension artifacts by copy when Windows locks the directory

On Windows a directory cannot be renamed while any process holds a handle inside a subdirectory of it, and the extension file watcher makes every running Qwen Code session hold exactly those handles. The existing retry makes four attempts inside about 350 ms, which cannot outlast a lock that lives as long as another session, so updating or uninstalling an extension never succeeded on such a machine.

A transaction now falls back to a copy-based swap: the installed tree is copied aside, the staged version is copied over it, and every path the new version no longer carries is pruned. The strategy the transaction used is recorded in its journal, so a rollback and a crash recovery follow the same direction instead of assuming the directory was renamed.

The copy strategy refuses what a rename could not reach. A destination whose real path leaves the extensions root, or that is not a real directory, is refused before anything is copied, because every walk reaches that root and readdir follows a link there; a copy-mode rollback then restores over the live tree rather than emptying it, so an entry it cannot delete leaves stale content instead of a destination without its manifest. Teardown removes what the strategy can leave behind: the half-published partial backup, and the backup a copy-mode rollback restored from. Timestamps survive the copies, and a swap that still cannot complete reports which directory is in use instead of a raw filesystem error.

* fix(core): harden the copy swap against held files and rewritten links

Review of the copy swap found three ways it could fail where a rename would not, all measured on Windows.

The copy steps lost the retry the rename path had: a scanner or an indexer holding one file transiently aborted a copy-mode update with a message that blames a session, on a path that used to absorb that case. The copies now go through one helper that retries EPERM/EBUSY four times inside about 350 ms, the shape the rename path uses.

fsp.cp rewrites a relative symlink target to an absolute path under the staging directory, which the commit then removes, so an extension carrying a relative link lost it. The copies pass verbatimSymlinks, which keeps the target as written, and the design doc now states that instead of the opposite.

A rollback that cannot complete used to leave its journal while every later operation re-ran that rollback before doing anything, so a holder that refused the restoring copy made every extension read and mutation fail until it let go. Recovery now keeps the journal and lets the operation proceed, retrying on the next one.

* fix(core): bound the extension recovery guard and order transaction replay

Reviewing the copy swap's recovery guard found it could certify a torn tree: a rollback that never completed left its journal unmarked, so the next operation that advanced the snapshot generation made recovery read that journal as committed and delete the only intact backup. The guard also swallowed every error and retried a whole-tree rollback on every operation.

A lock-defeated rollback is now marked in its journal, the generation leg ignores a marked journal, the failure is logged, and anything that is not a lock error still stops the caller. Stacked transactions for one destination are no longer possible - a second commit is refused while one is unresolved - and recovery replays pending journals newest first instead of in directory order, so the surviving content no longer depends on enumeration order.

The copy swap's deletions now retry the transient lock errors the copy does, a symlink re-creation failure is no longer classified as a held handle (the case that made the message wrong on a machine without symlink privilege), and each wrapped step names the directory it actually touches.

* fix(core): settle extension transactions instead of blocking on cleanup

Reviewing the recovery guard added in the previous commit found it conflating two
failures that leave different states. A lock error during teardown was recorded as
a blocked rollback, so a destination whose rollback had already restored kept
refusing later updates and re-copied its whole backup on every store operation.
Because the guard matched on journal existence rather than on the committed test
recovery uses, a transaction that had committed but could not delete its backup
refused later mutations on every platform. And a rename-mode rollback that could
not restore its destination was absorbed as well, which certifies an extension as
installed with no artifact directory behind it.

Recovery and the commit-side guard now share one predicate for "this transaction
still needs a rollback": committed, or restored with its backup left behind, or
past its target generation with no marker. Teardown is separated from the restore
- the staging tree, the backup a copy-mode rollback restored from, and an
unpublished partial backup - and a lock error there marks the journal
cleanupPending, so the retry repeats the removal rather than the restore. A
lock-defeated rollback is absorbed only while the destination still exists, and a
journal the holder blocked refuses with the actionable locked-directory message
instead of a bare transaction id.

Retries draw on one allowance per store operation rather than one per call, so a
tree whose entries are each transiently held ends in that message instead of
holding the store lock for a backoff per entry, and recovery reports a
transactions root it cannot enumerate instead of recovering nothing in silence.
The journal markers, the commit-side refusal and the corrected lock-hold bound are
documented in both languages.

* fix(core): settle blocked extension rollbacks with a self-healing retry window

A rollback defeated by a held directory is now settled rather than left to be
rediscovered on every store operation. The journal marker gained a retry
window: reads inside it stop re-attempting the restore, and once the window
passes the retry resumes on its own, so a destination heals when the holder
lets go instead of re-copying its whole tree behind every read or being
refused forever. The refusal branch - a rollback whose retry could not
produce a loadable artifact - now writes the marker before stopping the
caller, so even a refusal keeps its window and a later read rejects without
touching the tree.

What counts as a loadable artifact was corrected twice. Existence is not
integrity: the destination must still carry a manifest, not merely exist.
And one manifest name is not the loader's contract: Agent Plugins v1 are
installed unconverted with plugin.json at the root, so a gate recognising
only qwen-extension.json refused those extensions' rollbacks forever, off
the window's path entirely. The gate now accepts either root manifest, and
its probes treat any error - not just a missing path - as "not there", so a
destination a walk cannot enter is refused with the lock error kept as the
cause rather than crashing recovery with an unrelated errno.

Off Windows a permission denial is not a held handle, and the staged rename -
the one swap step that also runs on the rename path - had started reporting
one as a locked directory. The hint is now gated where it is actionable,
matching the sibling rename sites and the recovery refusal. Recovery
enumerates the transactions directory the way the merge base did, so a
transactions root that is a link no longer hides its journals from reads,
while the real-directory rule stays on the walks that delete. A cleanup that
failed for a non-lock reason is marked before its error reaches the caller,
so a later pass repeats the removal instead of restoring again from a
half-deleted backup.

* fix(core): judge blocked extension rollbacks by artifact integrity

* fix(core): absorb completed restores whose prune is still held

* fix(core): order journal replays by an immutable store-wide key

* fix(core): make the recovery loop's per-destination invariant structural

* fix(core): classify journal fate from mark and quarantine outcomes

The round-9 three-state machine in recoverTransactionsUnlocked treated recordPendingStep's mark-landed boolean and quarantineJournal's quarantined boolean inconsistently: the deferred-sibling branch returned the recordPendingStep value and continued silently; the catch set decided='unrecoverable' for any non-lock error before checking whether quarantineJournal had actually moved the journal; and the commit-side guard mirrored the same bugs. Round-9 review posted 3 new Criticals (R9-1, R8-1, R8-2) all rooted in that inconsistency.

* fix(core): key the replay order on a persisted key and keep faulted journals in the scan

R10-1: type the teardown spy's journal parameter as unknown. The interface it named is private to extension-store.ts, so naming it left packages/core unable to compile while the vitest suite stayed green.

R10-2: order same-generation journals by orderMs, stamped once (at creation, or from the observed mtime for journals written before the field) and never recomputed, instead of by the mtime a marking pass rewrites.

R8-2: stop quarantining a journal because an attempt failed. A failed attempt is evidence about the operation, not the file, so the journal keeps its name - it owns rollback/<id> and staging/<id> - and is marked instead; quarantine is now only reachable for a journal that cannot be parsed. recordPendingStep takes a reason rather than an error: every rollback mark opens a retry window, a recorded fault never claims a held directory, and the loop verdict carries the reason so older siblings always wait.

* fix(core): refuse a read while a faulted rollback is still owed

A journal marked by a fault was absorbed inside its retry window whenever the rollback-versus-backup comparison answered that a retry could still leave a loadable artifact, so a read reported the committed generation over a tree the rollback had never touched. Absorb is only sound for a step that actually ran: a journal recording a fault now goes through the same refusal as any other unresolved one, while a held step keeps absorbing so a completed restore is never redone.

The ordering witness pinned its premise with utimes rather than racing timestamp granularity, because the stamping pass rewrites both journals and leaves only a clock tick between them. It also asserts that every journal the pass orders persists its own key: without that check the computed-but-never-persisted case survives, since the older journal's key reaches disk as a side effect of the marking write.

feat(qqbot): Accept inbound images and videos (#12850)

QQ Bot was the only channel that ignored inbound media: an image-only or
video-only message was dropped before an envelope existed, and a media message
that carried a caption lost its attachment.

An image is now passed to the agent as vision input — it reaches the model in
the same prompt, so no tool call is needed to see it — and the same bytes are
also left on a temporary path with that path in the prompt, so a model that
cannot take images still has something to work with. A video is saved to a
temporary path and the agent is told that path. Only image/jpeg, image/png,
image/gif and video/mp4 are accepted, at most five attachments per message,
capped at 8 MB for images and 20 MB for videos, fetched over https from the
platform's own hosts. A media-only message becomes an `(image)` or `(video)`
placeholder marked as synthetic text, and a failed download reports itself
instead of dropping the message.

The channel documentation no longer states that QQ ignores inbound media.

fix(core): recover a failed reminder-less notification turn as interrupted_prompt (#13126)

* fix(core): recover a failed reminder-less notification turn as interrupted_prompt (#12042)

A delivered background-notification turn whose entry carries no reminders
is a single bare <task-notification> envelope — shape-identical to a cold
record the daemon persists before the turn runs, and stamped with the same
provenance: 'system' + subtype: 'notification'. When such a turn failed
mid-stream before any functionCall, the entry became the history tail and
the recovery trim ate it as if it were cold, certifying clean with no
Continue and no re-drive, so the background agent's terminal result never
reached the model (issue #12042 shape A).

Stamp the turn's own record deliveredTurn: true when client.ts sends it
(the only field that survives the channelTask admission branch, which runs
under backgroundTurnContext.exit and so cannot rely on backgroundTurn),
and have the api-history projection's per-entry notification flag count
only undelivered records. The delivered-but-unanswered entry now stays
classifiable and recovers as interrupted_prompt with a Retry continuation;
cold records still trim to clean, and the text-shape matcher remains the
fallback for metadata-free live-history callers.

fix(serve): release only load-owned Hook Runtimes (#13195)

* fix(serve): release only load-owned Hook Runtimes

releaseEarlierOwners() treated every activation in the Session log as a
Runtime owner. Each lifecycle Hook operation adds two activations (the
hook_operation one and its restore), so detach and the first operation
after a load sent one Broker release per historical Hook operation, and
parallel Hooks repeated the whole pass.

Only a load constructs a Hook owner, so the pass now skips hook_operation
activations and the activation the same worker installs on releasing
one. Activations installed by another worker, or after a hook_operation
activation that was never released, are loads after a failure and stay
owners. Execution runtimeSessionIds are unchanged. Parallel acquire()
calls now share one acquisition.

Fixes #13193

* fix(serve): ignore activation renewals when classifying Hook owners

renewActivation checks the phase before its append is serialized, so a
renewal timer that fires while a hook_operation release is committing
records the renewal after the release. The restore install then followed
an active event, so release took the restore for a load owner and sent
an extra release on every later load.

Renewals repeat their activation's identity and never name a new owner,
so the release pass now skips them without letting them become the prior
event. Tests cover a renewal after its install and one recorded after
the hook_operation release. A comment at the Hook operation activation
notes that Hosted Hook release depends on this order.

* fix(serve): identify Hook restore activations by a derived ID

The release pass took any activation the same worker installed after a
released hook_operation activation for the restore. When the restore
install failed and the same worker loaded the Session again, that load
was skipped. If it then acquired a Runtime without recording a Hook
execution (file history acquires directly) and crashed, nothing could
find its owner, and its hold was never released.

The Hook operation now installs its restore activation under a UUID
derived from the hook_operation activation's ID, and release skips
exactly those IDs. A load always installs a random ID, so it remains an
owner whatever precedes it. The classification no longer depends on
event order, worker IDs, or renewals.

replaceActivation() takes an optional activation ID for the successor.
Restores recorded before this change have random IDs; release treats
them as owners, and the Broker answers 404.

* fix(serve): derive the Hook restore ID from the replaced activation

The restore ID was derived from the hook_operation activation, so it
existed only once that activation installed. When the install failed,
the controller still restored an activation in its finally block, but
under a random ID; release then took the restore for a load owner and
sent an extra release on every later load.

Derive the restore ID from the activation the Hook operation replaced
instead. The log always holds that activation, so release recognizes
the restore whether or not the hook_operation activation installed.

* fix(core): refuse a repeated activation install and pin the restore ID

An activation install takes its command identity from the activation ID.
Installing an ID the log already holds therefore replayed the earlier
receipt without appending, and installActivation still returned a fresh
epoch that the log never recorded. Every later append would then fail the
actor fence. Hook restores are the first caller to name the ID, so refuse
the repeat with a conflict instead of letting it pass silently.

Pin managedHookRestoreActivationId to a literal. Writer and reader share
the function, so no in-process test noticed when its output changed, while
a later build must still recognize restores that an earlier one recorded.

State on replaceActivation what a named ID is for and that it must be new
to the log. Rename the it.each parameter that shadowed the released()
helper, and assert through the helper.

* test(serve): pass the managed session into the Hook operation helper

operate() built its activation controller from the outer session while
firing through the Hook session it was given. Take the managed session
as a parameter so each call names the pair it drives.

* fix(core): refuse a repeated activation ID before releasing the current one

replaceActivation() released the current activation and only then
learned, from the install, that the named successor ID was already in
the log. A refused repeat therefore left the session with no active
activation. Check the ID first, through a new hasInstalledActivation()
query. installActivation() also refuses the repeat before it publishes
the install body; its replay check stays for a concurrent repeat.

From the same audit rounds:
- test the route path: a DELETE that runs SessionEnd and SessionDelete
  releases only its own Hook Runtime;
- test a restore that replaces an unrestored hook_operation activation;
- state on the HostedHookSession constructor that it is built only on a
  load activation;
- note that the late-renewal test case depends on the core
  renewActivation race;
- docs: parallel acquisition is shared within one Hook session, and a log
  written before this change still costs each load one release per
  earlier Hook operation.

* refactor(core): share the repeated-activation refusal

The refusal for a repeated activation ID was built in two places:
`replaceActivation()` in the session assembly and `installActivation()`
in the authority. Export the authority's factory as
`activationAlreadyInstalledError()` and throw it from both, so the
message cannot drift. The assembly and authority tests now pin the
refusal's class and message at all three checks.

fix(core): stop misdiagnosing malformed tool-call args as max_tokens truncation (#12982)

* fix(core): stop misdiagnosing malformed tool-call args as max_tokens truncation

When a provider streams a fused/malformed tool-call argument bag, the
streaming parser flags the JSON as incomplete (brace depth > 0) and the
OpenAI converter unconditionally rewrites finish_reason to "length",
which turn.ts maps to wasOutputTruncated and the scheduler then appends
the max_tokens truncation note to the schema-validation error. The note
is asserted with no evidence: neither the provider's real finish_reason
nor usageMetadata is consulted, so a response that ended at 185
completion tokens is reported as token-limit truncation and the model
retries the identical call.

Guard the finish_reason override with the usage evidence: the pipeline
records the wire output budget (max_tokens or a provider-specific budget
key) on the request context, and the converter skips the override when
reported completion tokens fall well below that budget. Genuine
truncation (completion tokens at the cap, or usage/ceiling unavailable)
keeps the legacy inference, preserving the #4964 recovery path, and an
explicit provider-reported "length" is still trusted verbatim.

Refs #12970

Two defects in the #12970 corroboration guard, both reported on the review
thread at head 8b7848a:

R1-1 — the guard read `chunk.usage` off the chunk carrying `finish_reason`,
but this pipeline requests `stream_options.include_usage` (pipeline.ts:1079)
and under that convention the finish chunk reports no usage: the totals arrive
on a later `choices: []` chunk that `handleChunkMerging` folds into the parked
finish response. For that whole provider class the verdict was always
"inconclusive", the `stop` -> `length` rewrite fired exactly as before, and the
misdiagnosis this PR exists to remove still shipped. The converter now parks
the provider's own finish reason on the request context, and the pipeline
settles the rewrite on the parked response — before every one of its three
delivery points (post-merge yield, Stage 2d flush, error-path flush), so the
consumer only ever observes the settled reason. The park is reset when a
stream starts, because a retry can reuse the same context object.

R1-2 — only `undefined` counted as "no evidence", so a zero-filled usage object
(ModelScope sends exactly that on the finish chunk) or an explicit `null` fell
through to the ratio comparison and was read as proof *against* truncation.
That suppressed the #4964 override and, since `wasOutputTruncated` is the sole
key for the scheduler's reject-file-writes-while-truncated guard, disarmed it
on the responses it exists for — a truncated `write_file` repaired by jsonrepair
could then write a partial file. A missing, non-numeric or non-positive count
is now inconclusive rather than a disproof; it cannot mean "no output" here,
because this branch is only reached once the parser found incomplete JSON.

The corroboration helper becomes an exported three-state verdict so the
converter (chunk usage) and the pipeline (merged usageMetadata) share one
threshold and one notion of "no evidence".

50% threshold on both sides, and park / no-park. 252/252 pass.

fix(cli): use Linux-specific unavailable message for clipboard paste (#12504) (#12507)

* fix(cli): report clipboard unavailability on Linux instead of failing silently

clipboardHasImage() only invoked its onUnavailable callback on the
non-Linux path, when getClipboardModule() returned null. On Linux the
branch got tool === null from getLinuxClipboardTool() -- which returns
null at two separate points, once when there is no display server to
reach a tool through and once when the `command -v` probe throws --
matched neither wl-paste nor xclip, and fell through to `return false`
without notifying the caller.

Because InputPrompt's Ctrl+V matcher returns true unconditionally, the
keystroke was consumed with no feedback at all: "clipboard holds no
image" and "this machine has no clipboard backend" were
indistinguishable to the user.

Call onUnavailable?.() at the point where no Linux tool is available, so
the existing error-prompt path in InputPrompt fires on Linux too. One
call site covers both null exits since both return null from the same
function. Placement is deliberate: it sits after the two tool branches
and inside the try, so a tool that exists but reports no image still
returns false quietly rather than nagging users who only copied text.

Fixes #12488

feat(managed-agent): store immutable AgentDefinition revisions (Stage D8a) (#13142)

* feat(managed-agent): store immutable AgentDefinition revisions (Stage D8a)

Implement POST /v1/agents, GET /v1/agents/{agentId} and
POST /v1/agents/{agentId} as tenant-scoped, append-only revisions. The
server generates agent IDs; each revision carries the SHA-256 of its
canonical content, an update with unchanged content adds no revision, and
create and update replay or conflict under their Idempotency-Key. Flyway V27
adds the revision and command tables.

The tenant filter now also covers the bare /v1/agents path, which the
/v1/agents/ prefix check let through. Sessions still pin qwen-code and the
configured revision (D8b), and no definition field changes execution (D8c).
The contract moves the three routes to implemented at v1.29.0, assuming
#13112 lands v1.28 first.

* fix(managed-agent): replay concurrent identical AgentDefinition writes

The local verification on #13142 found that eight identical concurrent
creates answered one 202 and seven 409s: a duplicate command key surfaced
as idempotency_conflict although the same key and body must replay. A
write that loses a race now rolls back and reads the command committed
under its key, replaying it for the same request; a different request or
an unrecorded concurrent update keeps its 409.

Array items must be objects, so null items in tools, skills and
mcp_servers answer 400 instead of being stored, and the contract declares
skills, mcp_servers and metadata nullable, matching their treatment of
null as absent.

* fix(managed-agent): declare the replay header on AgentDefinition writes

createAgent and updateAgent answer 202 with X-Qwen-Idempotent-Replay, as
createSession, updateSession and unarchiveSession do, but the contract did
not declare it on the new routes. Declaring it also makes the contract test
require the header on both responses.

* docs(managed-agent): scope three design claims to what the code does

Corrects the D8a design doc (and its zh-CN twin) where it described
behavior the implementation does not have:

- §4.1 called the stored `definition_json` column the canonical JSON. It is
  written by the injected Spring ObjectMapper, while the row's digest comes
  from RequestDigests' alphabetically-sorted mapper, so sha256 of the column
  does not equal the digest. §4.2 keeps "canonical" for the digested form.
- §4.2 stated a universal "any other path ID answers 404 agent_not_found".
  Literal routes outrank `{agentId}`, so `/v1/agents/sessions` and
  `/v1/agents/workspaces` are answered by their own controllers. The
  operative conclusion (reserved names never resolve to a stored row) holds.
- §4.2 stated null-normalization as a general digest property. `content()`
  strips nulls one level only, so a null nested in an open map such as
  `metadata` does change the digest.

Docs only: no code, spec, or test changes. Verified by reading the sources
each sentence describes.

* fix(managed-agent): normalize tenant-filtered request paths

* fix(managed-agent): lock the head revision read in AgentDefinition update

update() decided "content equals the latest revision, so store nothing"
from a non-locking latest() read. The command lookup before it opens the
transaction's snapshot, so a revision committed in between is invisible:
a write whose content matched the stale head inserted nothing, neither
DuplicateKeyException branch could fire, and the route answered 202 with
a revision that was no longer the head. The command row then pinned that
Idempotency-Key to the stale revision, so every retry replayed it and the
write could never land.

Take the head read FOR UPDATE so the digest comparison and the revision
allocation both see the committed head, and concurrent updates of one
definition serialize. get() keeps the non-locking latest(), so reads do
not contend with writers. The SQL shape is the module's own:
ManagedToolResultStore.java:116 issues the same ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 FOR
UPDATE, exercised on H2 by ToolPublicationStoreTest.backfillOnePage.

The published updateAgent description and the design doc's concurrency
bullet both described the revision-number collision this replaces, so
both now state the serialized behavior. The 409 branch stays as a
fallback; idempotency_conflict is unchanged.

* docs(managed-agent): drop the stale single-revision claim from D2

D8a stores definition revisions, so the D2 session-query non-goal "Only
one agent revision exists until it lands" is now false, and the new D8a
page links D2 as a basis. Reword both language versions the way this
branch already reworded the D1 contract twin: definitions are stored,
Sessions keep pinning the configured revision until D8b.

main now has V31 (workspace recovery bundle) and V32 (workspace session
close), so this branch's V31 collided and failed the Flyway uniqueness lane.
Take the next free version.

@wenshao's real-stack run on MySQL 8.4 (REPEATABLE-READ) showed that

contested updates and 264 of 320 identical-request updates answered 500. He

byte-identical to the legal serial order (T2, then T1), so there is no lost
write to fix. Restore the plain head read and the docs and contract text that
describe it.

test(managed-agent): Disable MockMvc result printing in ManagedEventReplayTest (#13229)

With the default print mode, Spring Boot registers a result handler that
walks MockHttpServletResponse headers on the test thread after perform()
returns. Streaming flows then keep writing the response headers and body
from a background thread, so the walk occasionally hits a
ConcurrentModificationException — observed in CI as one red lane out of
428 managed-agent tests (expiredCursorsGetConflictOrOneResyncFrame).

Boot only registers that handler when print != MockMvcPrint.NONE, so
declaring print=NONE removes the only concurrent header reader. Mirrors
ManagedAgentApiContractTest, which received the same treatment in a
previous change.

overshoot is at most what a run spent since the previous pass (the host
ticks every second). A run a person triggered is left running, matching the
admission rule that a person's post passes the budget.

fix(web-shell): stop offering a Managed approval the viewer cannot answer (#13165)

* fix(web-shell): stop offering a Managed approval the viewer cannot answer

After the service answers 403 action_forbidden, the approval card kept its
Allow and Deny buttons enabled, so a viewer who is not the Session creator
could send one refused request per click until the Action expired. Disable
the card once that refusal arrives; the warning is scoped to the Action, so
the next approval is offered again.

* fix(web-shell): scope the creator-only approval latch to the Session

Review on #13165 found three gaps in the Managed approval refusal:

- action_forbidden is decided by the service from the (tenant, Session,
  actor) row on the respond path, but the disabled latch derived from the
  per-Action answerError, which the hook clears as soon as the refused
  Action leaves the pending list. A reader watching a Session that raises
  sequential approvals ate one guaranteed 403 per Action. The hook now
  keeps a Session-scoped respondForbidden flag, set on an action_forbidden
  answer failure and reset only when the selection changes, and the page
  disables the card from it; the per-Action warning keeps its scope.
- The persistent disabled state had no visual affordance: the only
  :disabled rule in ToolApproval.module.css is goal-scoped, so a refused
  Managed approval looked clickable while swallowing clicks. A base
  .option:disabled rule (after .option:hover so equal specificity resolves
  by source order) dims it and shows the not-allowed cursor; the goal
  variant's stronger rule is untouched.
- Every HTTP answer failure the client builds carries a string code, yet
  the only retry test used an uncoded Error, so nothing pinned that a
  coded but retryable failure stays answerable. A 503 negative control now
  fails if the action_forbidden condition is widened.

feat(core): resolve model limits and modalities from a models.dev catalog (#11959)

* feat(core): resolve model limits and modalities from a models.dev catalog

Bundle a trimmed models.dev snapshot (12 first-party providers, 237
models) and refresh it in the background once a day into
~/.qwen/model-registry.json with ETag revalidation, so a model that
appears on models.dev gets its context window, output limit, and input
modalities without a CLI release. tokenLimit()/knownTokenLimit()/
hasExplicitOutputLimit() consult the catalog before the regex tables;
defaultModalities() merges both so the catalog can only add modalities.

QWEN_CODE_MODELS_DEV=off restores the regex-only behavior (default in the
unit test setups), QWEN_CODE_MODELS_DEV_REFRESH=off disables the network
refresh, QWEN_CODE_MODELS_DEV_URL points at a mirror. `npm run
generate:model-catalog` regenerates the committed snapshot.

Implements PR2 and PR3 of the design in #9851. Refs #8558.

* feat(core): add model.customCatalog for offline model metadata

Offline and proxy-restricted users cannot reach models.dev, so let them
point `model.customCatalog` at a URL or local file whose entries are
merged over the bundled catalog per model and field. Both the trimmed
`{ models: { id: entry } }` shape and models.dev-style payloads are
accepted. A file is re-read synchronously at every start so the first
model resolution already sees it; a URL is cached like models.dev and
is still fetched when QWEN_CODE_MODELS_DEV_REFRESH=off. The cache
records its source, so a changed or removed setting drops the overlay.

Also sort snapshot keys with a plain comparator instead of localeCompare
so regeneration is deterministic across machines.

* docs: add a verification brief for the models.dev catalog

CI covers the mechanism, but every unit test stubs fetch and the test
setups run with the catalog off, so neither the data values nor the real
runtime behavior are verified anywhere. This brief is the handoff for a
machine that can run the CLI against live endpoints: an on/off A/B with
measured reference numbers, the refresh and offline paths, and the two
values that may still be wrong (Anthropic 1M context, qwen3.8-max PDF).

* fix(core): only catalog models the endpoint question has one answer for

Two projection bugs, both found by reviewing the magnitude of the changes
the catalog was making rather than their direction.

The provider whitelist filtered by vendor but never by model type, so the
catalog also carried embedding, text-to-speech, image, video, OCR and
translation models whose limits mean something else entirely:
gemini-embedding-001 reported an output limit of 1 and veo-3.1-generate a
context of 480, and those numbers outranked the family fallbacks that keep
such ids harmless today. Require tool calling and text output, which drops
34 ids and no real chat model.

Conflict resolution picked the vendor's numbers when several providers
served one id, but a context window is a property of the endpoint, not the
weights. DashScope caps GLM-5 output at 16,384 where Z.ai allows 131,072;
both are correct for their own endpoint. Worse, kimi-k2.6 has no matching
output pattern today, so it is treated as unknown and the user's max_tokens
is respected, and the catalog would have clamped it to 262,144. Drop such
ids instead of guessing: 220 of 237 ids have no conflict, and the 11 that
remain keep exactly the answer they get today.

Snapshot goes from 237 models to 192, 29,824 to 24,685 bytes.

* fix(web-shell): stop the memory panel replacing a global QWEN.md it could not read

The memory panel's User tab read ~/.qwen/QWEN.md through the sandboxed
GET /file, which refuses anything outside the bound workspace. The read
failed quietly, the editor opened empty, and Save sent mode=replace to
POST /workspace/memory, which accepts the global scope and overwrote the
whole file with whatever was typed (#13100).

- GET /workspace/memory (and the _qwen/workspace/memory ACP method) take
  an opt-in content flag that returns each discovered file's text, capped
  at the write route's 1 MB limit with a truncated marker. The paths are
  the ones the daemon itself discovers, so this exposes nothing the write
  route cannot already replace.
- useDaemonMemory gains readMemoryFile, which reads through that flag and
  falls back to the file API on daemons that predate it.
- The panel stays read-only (Edit and Save disabled, save handler
  refuses) whenever an existing file's full text is not in hand: a failed
  read or truncated content. A failed global read shows the existing
  memory.globalReadUnsupported message instead of the raw
  "path escapes workspace" error.

Not run locally: vitest, typecheck and eslint are left to CI. Prettier
(--experimental-cli) passes on the changed files.

Fixes #13100

* fix(memory): gate replace on a loaded file list, refuse lossy decodes

Two paths still let the memory panel offer mode=replace over bytes it
did not actually have:

- `editable` defaulted to true, so while the memory-status load was
  outstanding `files` was empty and the create path opened Edit + Save
  over a file that was really on disk (the destructive step in the
  linked issue). Gate on the load having succeeded
  (`status !== undefined`), never on `files` being empty, so the
  legitimate first-memory-file create path keeps working.
- the content read decoded with a bare `.toString('utf8')`, so a
  GBK/Shift_JIS/UTF-16LE file came back as U+FFFD text that still
  looked complete, and the first Save rewrote the real bytes with no
  backup. Decode with `fatal: true` and omit `content` when the buffer
  is not valid UTF-8, so the client falls back to the encoding-aware
  file route instead.

Line-ending preservation across the content flag needs a wire field and
is tracked separately; it is not attempted here.

* fix(web-shell): make the memory save CRLF restoration idempotent

The CRLF arm added in d4de16b2ee keyed its expansion on `\n`, but
`restoreCrlf` is derived from `content` while the expansion is applied to
`draft`. On a save with zero keystrokes `draft` still holds the file's raw
CRLF text — `loadContent` seeds it with `setDraft(result.content)`, and a
programmatic React value normalizes only the textarea's DOM value, never
the state — so Edit then Save rewrote every line ending as CR-CR-LF and
`mode:'replace'` wrote that to disk with no backup. `setContent(payload)`
then re-seeded the guard with text that still passes the uniform-CRLF
test, so each further no-op save added another CR per line.

Expanding `/\r?\n/g` instead makes the restoration idempotent: an
LF-normalized (typed) draft still gains the file's CRLF endings, and an
untouched CRLF draft round-trips unchanged. The uniform-CRLF condition on
`content` is kept, so mixed-ending files are still never re-expanded.

* ci(sdk-java): guard Flyway version uniqueness and watch red main runs

Two in-flight PRs each added a V16 managed-agent-server migration and
merged 23 minutes apart; each branch was green in isolation, and Flyway
refused to boot the merged result, leaving main red for two hours while
three more merges stacked on it (#12940).

A new flyway-migrations job runs scripts/check-flyway-migrations.js on
every SDK Java pull request and push: a filename scan of the two
migration locations that share one version sequence, failing in seconds
and naming both files when two claim one version. Versions compare the
way Flyway compares them — numerically per segment — so V016 collides
with V16, and a location rename that would empty the guard fails instead
of passing vacuously.

The main-CI failure watcher now watches the SDK Java workflow, whose
path-filtered push run on main is the only signal for a merge result
neither PR could fail, and the failure-signature helper reads Surefire's
per-test error lines, so a red Java lane files one deduped issue naming
the failing tests instead of a per-commit stub.

* ci(sdk-java): harden the Flyway guard and dedupe its main-red issues

Review on #12965:

- compare versions across every module of one invocation — Flyway resolves
  classpath:db/migration across jars, so a version claimed in two modules
  collides exactly like two files in one module
- fail when the SQL location yields no migration even if the Java location
  still does, so renaming one location away can no longer pass vacuously
- escape %/CR/LF in module names and file paths before emitting ::error::
  (the runner parses workflow commands from stderr too, and the job scans
  contributor-controlled filenames on pull_request)
- match the migration suffix case-insensitively, as Flyway does
- keep the fully qualified Surefire id as the dedupe identity so same-named
  tests in different packages no longer merge into one issue; the cosmetic
  package strip moves to shortenForTitle
- give the guard's ::error:: line a stable flyway:<module>:<version>
  identity, so a standing red dedupes to one issue instead of one per
  stacked merge, and render the failed jobs in the test-keyed body
- pin the workflow_run watch entry to sdk-java.yml's name key

* ci(sdk-java): fix the Flyway dedupe on runner-rendered logs and close review findings

The Actions runner consumes ::error:: workflow commands and writes
##[error] into the downloadable job log, so the dedupe pattern anchored
on ^::error:: never matched production input and every merge stacked on
a standing red would have opened a fresh autofix issue. The anchor now
accepts both forms, the guard's two non-collision failure modes (moved
migration location, missing module directory) get their own stable
module+mode identity, and the synthesized flyway id is written to be
read since it doubles as the issue title and body bullet.

The issue body's "- Failed jobs:" block is now machine-owned like
"## Also failing": stripped and re-emitted from the current run on every
merge instead of freezing the lanes recorded at filing time, with the
empty-list case pinned against a dangling heading.

The guard itself now reports a multi-module collision once after all
modules are scanned, naming every claimant (a second line would file a
second issue), never prints a clean summary for a claimant, and only
requires the SQL location of a module that owns a db/migration*
directory — which lets the workflow invocation cover runtime-broker, the
module that shares the classpath:db/migration namespace without carrying
migrations today.

escapeWorkflowCommand moves to scripts/release-script-utils.js (the
byte-identical copy would have drifted from the tested original), and
the filename-forgery tests gain a runner-decoding oracle and a
capability probe so the Windows lane skips instead of failing on

* ci(sdk-java): close the guard's blind spots and validate its dedupe captures

Review and sandboxed verification on #12965 found the moved-location
probe keying on the two exact directory names: a rename outside the
migration* family (db/migration -> db/changelog) passed silently with
the whole sequence inside it, a renamed Java location printed "all
versions unique" from a scan that skipped it, and a Java-only module
red-lit as "moved" with its real collision never named. The probe is
now derived from the LOCATIONS table: a versioned-migration file
anywhere under a source root but outside the configured location fails
with the files named, the sibling check is per location and fires only
when the location directory itself is gone, and a repeated module
argument no longer fabricates a collision of a file with itself.

The invocation now names qwencode too — managed-agent-server depends on
it at compile scope, the same namespace premise that admitted
runtime-broker — and the .size-baseline entry is re-recorded at the
file's current size.

On the consumer side, both Flyway patterns feed their captures through a
module-shape validation before they become a dedupe identity, so a
filename-borne forgery rendered by the runner's annotation decode can no
longer inject a second identity into the issue this files, and the
guard's run-level diagnosis is ordered ahead of first-seen test ids so a
mass failure in another lane cannot crowd it past the search and body
caps. A closure pin keeps the spawned guard importable in the
dependency-free helper lane.

Refs #12940

* ci(sdk-java): close the Windows-drive forgery and split the stray-file message

The drive-prefix alternative in the module validator re-opened the
forgery it closed: backslash and colon are ordinary characters in a
POSIX filename, so a migration name could supply a `C:\evil` prefix and
pass the path-shape check. No lane that runs this consumer ever
produces a backslashed module — the producer and analyze jobs are
ubuntu-latest and the suite runs only on the Linux lint_and_static
lane — so the branch is dropped, backslashes are rejected outright, and
the fixtures hand the guard a slash-bearing argument (a no-op on POSIX)
instead of teaching the consumer a shape only a forgery can produce.
The unsafe-character half of the validator is now pinned for
whitespace, backticks and backslashes across both call sites.

A populated location with a migration-shaped stray elsewhere under the
source root no longer prints "found no migration under": the guard
names the stray as the cause, and the consumer's config identity learns
the new phrase, so the standing red still files one issue. The dep-free
closure pin now walks the guard's relative-import closure instead of a
hardcoded depth-one list, so a new hop carrying an npm import cannot
slip through.

The rebase onto 51b80dadbc folded #12945's Hosted latency steps into the
