fix(file): guard default-open against paths the OS cannot chdir into (#21248)

### What this PR does

Before this PR: clicking a local-file path chip whose folder does not
exist killed a process with `SIGTRAP` on Linux. Electron's Linux
`shell.openPath()` forks a child, `chdir`s it into `dirname(path)` and
only then execs `xdg-open`; Chromium treats a failing `chdir` as a fatal
`RAW_CHECK` (`int3` → `SIGTRAP`/`SI_KERNEL`). The dying process is a
pre-exec fork, so it still looks like a CherryStudio instance while
Crashpad, `child-process-gone` and the app log see nothing. A path chip
can carry such a path in two ways: it is workspace-relative
(`assets/logo.png`), or it is stale/absolute with a parent directory
that no longer exists.

After this PR: the file module's default-open primitive refuses any
target that is not an existing absolute path, every raw-path entry point
funnels through it, and agent sessions resolve workspace-relative paths
in main from the session's own workspace. Unopenable links now surface
the existing `chat.input.tools.open_file_error` toast instead of taking
a process down.

Fixes #21226

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The guard sits in `safeOpen()` (`src/main/services/file/system.ts`)
rather than at each call site, because the call sites differ only in
where the string came from: `FileManager.open`, `ExternalAppService`,
the legacy `file:openPath` channel, `system.shell.open_path` and the
`http://file/` window-open intercept all end in the same
`shell.openPath`. One `fs.stat` (via the existing `getPathStatus`) both
proves the path is usable and discharges the `chdir` precondition, since
an existing target always has a traversable parent.

Resolution lives in main, not the renderer: a renderer can only
string-join `${workspacePath}/${path}`, so it cannot know whether the
result exists — and when an agent reports a path relative to its own cwd
(e.g. `<ws>/src`), that join produces a path that still does not exist
and still crashes. The new `ai.agent.session.open_path` route looks the
workspace up from the session row, so the renderer only ever forwards
the path text it was given.

The following tradeoffs were made: `system.shell.open_path` and the
`http://file/` intercept now inherit the dangerous-extension policy that
`file.open` already enforced (a behaviour change, in the safe
direction). Callers that `void` the `system.shell.open_path` request
(notes menu, dependency settings) can now see a rejected promise where
the failure used to be swallowed; they should decide whether to surface
it, which is left as a follow-up rather than bundled here.

The following alternatives were considered: spawning `xdg-open`
ourselves to bypass Electron's `chdir` (rejected: reimplements platform
dispatch, drops the Wayland activation token, and adds a native spawn
surface for a one-line precondition); accepting a renderer-supplied base
directory to resolve against (rejected: makes the renderer the authority
for path resolution); adding a `file.open_path` IpcApi route (rejected:
unused surface while the preload still exposes the legacy channel for
home chat).

Links to places where the discussion took place: #21226. Electron's
implementation is `shell/common/platform_util_linux.cc::OpenPath`
(`XDGOpen(full_path.DirName(), ...)`), and the fatal check is
`base/process/launch_posix.cc` (`RAW_CHECK(chdir(current_directory) ==
0)`), with `base/immediate_crash.h` emitting `int3` on x86.

### Breaking changes

No API breaks. Behaviour changes, all in the safe direction:

- Opening a path that does not exist, or is relative, now fails with
`FILE_OPEN_TARGET_UNAVAILABLE` (shown as the existing "could not open
this file" toast) instead of silently doing nothing or crashing.
- `system.shell.open_path` and the `http://file/` intercept now apply
the same dangerous-extension policy as `file.open`.
- Relative path chips in home chat are rejected: that surface has no
workspace to resolve against.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- Root cause reproduced locally against Electron 41.8.0 before the fix:
a target with a missing parent directory prints `Check failed:
chdir(current_directory) == 0` (strace: `chdir("...") = -1 ENOENT`),
while the same target with an existing parent directory opens normally.
- Re-checked after merging `main`, which moves the app to Electron
44.2.0: `shell/common/platform_util_linux.cc::OpenPath` still passes
`full_path.DirName()` and `base/process/launch_posix.cc` still has
`RAW_CHECK(chdir(current_directory) == 0)`, so the precondition is
unchanged and this guard is still load-bearing.
- The branch is merged with `main`; conflicts were import-block only
(`ipc/handlers/ai.ts`, its test, `MainWindowService.ts`). Typecheck, the
file/IPC suites and the touched renderer suites were re-run on the
merged tree.
- Regression test: `INT-3h` asserts a missing target rejects with
`FILE_OPEN_TARGET_UNAVAILABLE` and never reaches `shell.openPath`.
`INT-3g` previously asserted an open for an entry whose file was never
written to disk, so it now materializes the file first.
- `src/main/services/FileStorage.ts` is deliberately untouched. Its
`openPath` becomes unreachable once the legacy channel binds to
`openRequestPath`; it is left in place because the file is already
`@deprecated` and slated for deletion. Its existing test now uses a real
temporary file.
- `ReportArtifacts.tsx` needs no change: it calls `openArtifactFile`
directly and never routes a system open through `openFileTarget`.
- `skill.folder.open` and the miniApp activity-log folder open still
call `shell.openPath` directly; they open directories they own or just
created, so they cannot hit this failure mode. Centralizing them is a
follow-up, not part of this fix.
- Known gap, unchanged by this PR: in the agent host `ClickableFilePath`
still calls `isDirectory` before `openPath`, and that pre-check throws
when the renderer has no workspace loaded, so main never gets the chance
to resolve.

### What this PR does

Before this PR:

In Pi's `auto` permission mode, the rtk rewrite (step 4 of
`createPiToolAuthorizer`) mutated `input.command` in place before
`requiresApproval` ran `detectDestructiveCommand`. With rtk installed,
`git push --force` became `rtk git push --force`, the detector resolved
the command word as `rtk`, and the command ran without a prompt. The
same applied to every rule keyed on the command word (`git`, `find`,
`docker`, …). Code Mode's nested calls share the same authorizer, so
they were affected too.

After this PR:

`createPiToolAuthorizer` takes a shallow copy of the model-issued input
before the rewrite and passes it to `requiresApproval`, so `auto` mode
classifies the command the model actually wrote. The approval card and
the executed command are still the rewritten one, so the user approves
exactly what runs.

<!-- (optional, in `fixes #<issue number>(, fixes #<issue_number>, ...)`
format, will close the issue(s) when PR gets merged)*: -->

Fixes #

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Classification relies on rtk's rewrite preserving command semantics
(it only compacts output). A rewrite that turned a harmless command into
a destructive one would not be caught, but rtk is a user-installed
trusted binary that already executes every command.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Adding `rtk` to the detector's `WRAPPERS` set: a one-word change, but
it couples detection to rtk's output grammar (any rewrite to a different
subcommand name, or a `rtk proxy …` form, would silently bypass the
rules again).
- Moving the rtk rewrite after the approval decision: the card would
show `git push --force` while `rtk git push --force` runs, breaking
"approve what executes". The Claude runtime also rewrites before
approval (PreToolUse hook before `canUseTool`), so the current order
stays consistent across runtimes.

Before: `AiSdkToGeminiSse` emitted `usageMetadata` without
`cachedContentTokenCount`, and `applyUsageMetadata()` ignored
`stats.inputTokenDetails.cacheReadTokens`. A cached turn (prompt 30
incl. 10 cache-read, output 20 with 5 thoughts) produced:

```

```

After: the same turn reports the cache subset on Gemini's own field:

```
promptTokenCount: 30, candidatesTokenCount: 15, totalTokenCount: 50,
thoughtsTokenCount: 5, cachedContentTokenCount: 10
```

`promptTokenCount` stays the cache-inclusive prompt total (Gemini's
semantics, which the frame invariant guarded by #21238 already relies
on), so `cachedContentTokenCount` is a subset of the prompt — the sum
`prompt + candidates + thoughts` is untouched. The field is emitted only
when the projection carries a non-zero count, mirroring the file's
existing `thoughtsTokenCount > 0` convention.

- The projection carries the subset by contract — `GatewayUsageMetadata`
documents that the gateway adapters read "the cache-read and reasoning
breakdowns for dialects that expose them" — and the pinned Google
provider fills it straight from Gemini's own field: `@ai-sdk/google`
3.0.113 maps `inputTokens = { total: promptTokenCount, noCache:
promptTokenCount − cachedContentTokenCount, cacheRead:
cachedContentTokenCount ?? 0 }`.

for it; without this the gateway's Gemini-compatible endpoint never
reports cache hits, so cache hit rates and cached-token billing are
invisible to clients even when the upstream reported them.
- The sibling adapters forward the same projection field: OpenAI Chat →
`prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens`, Anthropic →
`cache_read_input_tokens` (#21260), Responses →
`input_tokens_details.cached_tokens` (#21266). The Gemini dialect was
the remaining gap in the usage matrix.

treats the totals: #21238 established `total = prompt + candidates +

reads on their own field keeps that invariant intact.

fix(api-gateway): split cache reads and writes out of the Anthropic input_tokens (#21261)

Fixes #21260

### What this PR does

Before: `AiSdkToAnthropicSse` emitted the `message-metadata`
projection's `stats.inputTokens` — the AI SDK v6 semantic of **total
input including cache reads and writes** — as the Anthropic frame's
`input_tokens`, with `cache_read_input_tokens: null` and
`cache_creation_input_tokens: 0`. A cached turn (12 uncached + 200
cache-read + 100 cache-write = 312 projected total) produced:

```
input_tokens: 312, cache_read_input_tokens: null, cache_creation_input_tokens: 0
```

The Anthropic usage semantics are the opposite split: `input_tokens` is
the uncached portion and cache reads/writes are reported separately
(billed input = `input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens +
cache_read_input_tokens`). Clients applying the field semantics saw no
cache usage at all and cost the whole 312 at the uncached rate.

After: the adapter splits the projected total — `input_tokens` becomes
the uncached portion (derived as `total − read − write`) and the
breakdown is forwarded, so the same turn now produces `input_tokens: 12,
cache_read_input_tokens: 200, cache_creation_input_tokens: 100` (sum =
312, the frame-internal invariant `input_tokens + cache_creation +
cache_read = projected total` holds). Without a projected breakdown,
today's behavior is kept (`input_tokens` = total, buckets at their SDK
defaults).

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

- The projection the adapter consumes is cache-inclusive by design.
Pinned `@ai-sdk/anthropic` 3.0.125 maps `convertAnthropicMessagesUsage`
as `inputTokens: { total: inputTokens + cacheCreationTokens +
cacheReadTokens, noCache, cacheRead, cacheWrite }`, and main's own
runtime projections state the same contract
(`src/main/ai/runtime/claudeCode/streamAdapter.ts`: "Top-level
`inputTokens` follows the v6 semantic of TOTAL input (cache reads and
writes included)").
- The adapter's previous comment ("The UIMessageChunk usage projection
carries no cache-token breakdown") no longer held:
`GatewayUsageMetadata.stats.inputTokenDetails` documents the breakdown,
the runtime emits `noCacheTokens/cacheReadTokens/cacheWriteTokens` on
the wire, and the sibling OpenAI adapter already reads `cacheReadTokens`
into `prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` — the Anthropic dialect is
the one that natively exposes these fields.
- Splitting (rather than only forwarding the read count) keeps the
frame-internal sum consistent; forwarding the breakdown on top of the
cache-inclusive total would double-count cache reads.
- `GatewayUsageMetadata.stats.inputTokenDetails` is extended with the
`noCacheTokens` / `cacheWriteTokens` fields the runtime already emits —
the interface type previously narrowed them away. The write bucket stays
adapter-local (`state.cacheReadTokens` remains the shared field used by
the OpenAI adapter).

(read + write) and the non-streaming usage (read only); an existing test

fix(deepseek-harness): accept relative and absolute Location in the 303 readiness probe (#21271)

### What this PR does

Before this PR:

Managed DeepSeek Harness launches fail against dsh **0.1.7-rc.2** with
`DeepSeek Harness Web UI returned HTTP 303`. The readiness probe
compared the token-exchange redirect target verbatim
(`response.headers.get('location') === '/'`), and dsh 0.1.7-rc.2 now
emits the relative form `Location: ./` (see
`@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-connection/lib/index.js` lines 405/415). The
relative form is legal per RFC 9110 section 10.2.2 and resolves against
the request URL to the same root resource, so the verbatim comparison
was the brittle part.

After this PR:

The probe resolves the `Location` header against the probe URL instead
of string-comparing it. All three equivalent spellings pass the token
exchange — legacy `/`, relative `./` (dsh 0.1.7-rc.2), and an absolute
loopback URL — while a 303 resolving anywhere else (e.g. `/admin`) or an
unusable header still rejects readiness, so the guard does not get
looser.

Fixes #21132

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

The following tradeoffs were made:

- Resolution-based comparison (`new URL(location, readyUrl)` vs `new
URL('/', readyUrl)`) keeps accepting exactly the same resource the old
check accepted, so the security posture of the readiness gate is
unchanged — it still only token-exchanges when the redirect stays on the
probed root.
- An unusable `Location` header (unparseable URL) resolves to `false`
instead of throwing, so failure keeps surfacing as the regular `Web UI
returned HTTP 303` diagnostic rather than a raw `Invalid URL` error.

The following alternatives were considered:

- Fixing the DSH side to emit `/` again (the reporter verified this
works) — but the robust fix belongs on the client side, since any
harness upgrade reinstalls the bundled copy and reintroduces the
failure.
- `location === '/' || location === './'` — narrower diff, but it
re-encodes the same brittle string matching for any future spelling;
resolution is one expression and covers the protocol semantics.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- Tests: `before` red evidence — with the fix reverted, the two new
acceptance cases (`Location: ./` and absolute `Location:
http://127.0.0.1:43123/`) fail with exactly the issue's error message; a
third case asserts a 303 to `/admin` is still rejected, and it stays
green before and after (guard not loosened). A broken-implementation
spot check (target changed to `/broken-on-purpose`) turned 3 cases red,
confirming the new tests bite.

fix(agent-right-pane): bound workspace tree depth and gate Files on any entry (#21255)

> ### Branch strategy
>
> - Active development targets `main`.

### What this PR does

Before this PR: opening an agent session whose workspace is a real
repository could freeze the whole window for ~20 s. The agent right pane
created a directory tree for every SYSTEM workspace — unconditionally,
regardless of which right-pane tab was open — using
`ARTIFACT_MISSING_WORKSPACE_TREE_OPTIONS`, which carried no `maxDepth`.
That installed a full-depth ripgrep scan plus a recursive chokidar
watcher over the entire workspace (17,227 watch handles on the reported
workspace, while ~2,900 was already enough to exhaust the process fd
budget). The watcher hit `EMFILE`, and the fallback in
`src/main/services/file/watcher.ts` then tore the native watcher down
synchronously on the main thread. The Files readiness gate also required
a *file* node, so a workspace containing only directories lost its Files
tab entirely.

After this PR: the initial workspace tree is bounded to one level, and
Files readiness is based on any entry rather than a file. The watcher
stays small (17,227 → 136 handles on the same workspace, measured on the
running build), and a directory-only workspace keeps its Files tab.

Fixes # (no upstream issue exists for this — EMFILE / chokidar / watcher
/ workspace-tree searches return nothing related)

### Why we need it and why it was done in this way

Evidence from the reported case (release 2.1.3, macOS, one agent
session):

- The app log recorded `chokidar native watcher hit EMFILE; falling back
to polling` 21 times in a single day, always naming that session's
worktrees; the main-process log goes silent for 23 s immediately after
one of them while the app was otherwise logging every ~5 s.
- A DevTools CPU profile of the freeze shows 22.0 s of self time in the
native `close` frame reached from chokidar's `FSWatcher.close` — on the
**main process** thread. The renderer stayed idle (24.1 s `(idle)`),
which is exactly why compositor animations kept playing while every
click died: IPC was starved, not the UI thread.

The following tradeoffs were made:

- **Initial tree depth 3 → 1.** Only level 1 is rendered while folders
are collapsed (the tree only walks children of expanded ids, and only
the workspace root is pre-expanded), so the deeper initial scan was pure
prefetch — expansion already loads children on demand through
`listDirectoryEntries(recursive: false)` plus a depth-1 watcher per
expanded folder. Cost: expanding a folder shows its children after one
lazy round trip instead of instantly.
- **Readiness counts entries, not files.** A directory-only workspace is
still browsable (folders expand lazily), and "any entry at level 1" is
equivalent to "the workspace is not empty" because any deeper entry has
an ancestor at level 1. Note it means any *non-ignored* entry: a
workspace holding only `node_modules`/dot-dirs stays unavailable, as
before.

The following alternatives were considered:

- **Progressive deepening (3 → 6 → … → 30 until a file appears).**
Rejected: each step rebuilds the builder and its watcher (a different
`maxDepth` is a different builder key), the trigger fires hardest for a
missing/empty root — the `watchMissingRoot` case — and the terminal
state is effectively the unbounded watcher again (depth 6 alone is
~12.4k handles on the reported workspace, depth 9+ ~17.2k). It also
cannot succeed when the only files live under ignored directories, which
are never reported at any depth.
- **A one-shot deep probe (`listDirectoryEntries(recursive: true)`)
instead of counting entries.** Viable if "must be a file, anywhere" were
a hard requirement, but it costs a full-depth scan and loses the live
flip when the first entry appears.

Links to places where the discussion took place: None

### Breaking changes

None. Renderer-only; no schema, migration, or main-process surface
changes.

### Special notes for your reviewer

- The readiness rename is `hasSystemWorkspaceFiles` →
`hasSystemWorkspaceEntries`; the only behavior change is that a SYSTEM
workspace with entries but no files at the loaded depth now offers the
Files tab (its pinned test was updated accordingly).
- Residual, intentionally out of scope: level-1 fan-out is still
unbounded (a workspace with thousands of level-1 directories still
creates thousands of watches), and `watcher.ts` still tears the watcher
down synchronously on the main thread when `EMFILE` does occur. This PR
shrinks the trigger by ~127× and makes the teardown ~6× cheaper; it does
not remove the class.

This checklist is not enforcing, but it's a reminder of items that could
be relevant to every PR.

Fixed a freeze when opening an agent session whose workspace is a large repository: the workspace file tree no longer watches the whole tree unboundedly, and a workspace containing only folders keeps its Files tab.

fix(github): never auto-select metadata assets as the tool (#13908)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/393

mise's automatic GitHub asset selection could pick a metadata file, such
as an SBOM, signature or checksum, as the tool. Releases that publish
platform-tagged metadata (for example
`editorconfig-checker-darwin-all.tar.gz.sbom.json` next to the real
archives) have assets whose names carry the same OS and architecture
tokens as the real binary. Metadata files were only penalized by 100
points, so one could still score above zero and be chosen, installed as
the tool, and recorded in `mise.lock`.

mise writes always points at a real archive or binary. For

github:editorconfig-checker/editorconfig-checker@4.0.2` installs the
platform archive and never an `.sbom.json`.

Metadata is recognized by a shared `is_metadata_asset` helper (`.json`,
`.jsonl`, `.intoto.jsonl`, `.sbom`, `.sig`, `.sha256`, `.pem`, and
similar suffixes) that the existing scoring penalty now also uses.
Explicit `url` and `asset_pattern` options do not go through automatic
selection, so they are unaffected and can still name any file.

fix(task): let tasks shut down after a single Ctrl-C (#13904)

A single Ctrl-C during `mise run` could make mise exit right away and
kill tasks that were still cleaning up. The shell prompt came back while
child processes were still stopping, so their output landed on top of
it.

This happened in three situations:

- **A task runs `mise run` itself.** The inner mise got the SIGINT
twice, once from the terminal and once from the outer mise, and took the
second as a repeated Ctrl-C.
- **A task needs a single SIGINT to shut down cleanly.** `docker compose
up` stops gracefully on the first SIGINT and force-quits on the second.
- **A task exits non-zero on SIGINT** instead of dying by it, as
`aws-vault` and many CLIs do. mise counted that as an ordinary failure
and sent SIGTERM to the other tasks mid-shutdown.

Repro:

```toml
[tasks.slow]
run = "trap '' INT; sleep 6; date > done.txt"

[tasks.outer]
run = "mise run slow"
```

Run `mise run outer` in a terminal and press Ctrl-C once.

- **Before:** mise exits immediately with status 130, `slow` is killed,
and `done.txt` is never written.
- **After:** mise waits for `slow` to finish, writes `done.txt`, then
exits with status 130.

A second Ctrl-C still force-quits, as before.

### Changes

- `CmdLineRunner::kill_all` no longer re-sends SIGINT to children that
share mise's process group when that SIGINT has already reached them:
from the terminal, or from an outer mise that owns the group and signals
all of it with `killpg`. Children in their own process group or session
are still signalled.
- On Linux, mise records where each SIGINT came from, so a `kill -INT
<mise pid>` that reaches mise alone is still passed on to every task.
The record is only ever set by a SIGINT and cleared by `kill_all`, so a
second SIGINT arriving first cannot hide it.
- The per-command signal forwarder no longer forwards SIGINT; `kill_all`
from the Ctrl-C handler already does.
- A Ctrl-C no longer triggers the "task failed, killing siblings"
SIGTERM. The SIGINT handler marks the run as cancelled itself, so the
check doesn't lag behind a task that took the same SIGINT and exited
non-zero first.

### Behavior notes

- **macOS:** macOS reports a terminal Ctrl-C and `kill -INT`
identically, so a `kill -INT <mise pid>` sent while mise is in the
terminal's foreground is no longer passed to children in mise's process
group. Ctrl-C is unaffected.
- **Nested mise:** a `kill -INT` sent to a nested `mise run` alone is
not passed on to its tasks, because a nested mise assumes its outer
mise's group-wide signal already reached them.
- **Linux:** `kill -INT -<pgid>` and `kill -INT <pid>` look the same to
mise, so a SIGINT sent to the whole group can reach children twice. A
duplicate beats a lost signal that leaves mise waiting on a task.

### Testing

New e2e tests, all driving real signals: a pty Ctrl-C through a nested
`mise run`, the same nesting with no terminal (the task must see exactly
one SIGINT, which fails without the nested-mise check), a sibling that
exits non-zero on SIGINT, and a process-directed `kill -INT` (Linux
only). The four tests pass on macOS (the last skips there). The
Linux-only code paths were not compiled locally; CI covers them.

Based on #13895 by @thebengeu, whose diagnosis and tests this builds on.
This PR adds the nested-mise case, the missed-SIGINT-origin race, and
the no-tty test.

docs: stop the showreel's dark gradients from banding into rings (#13902)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/389
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

The landing-page showreel showed faint, slightly rainbow-tinted rings in
its dark backgrounds. They were sharpest around the chef's glow on the
end card, where they swept outward as the glow swelled ("blooming"), and
in the stage lamp at the open and during the chef morph. This change
removes them, so those areas now look smooth and grainy as drawn.

**Cause.** The lamp, the vignette and the glows are huge, soft gradients
on a near-black stage. Each one climbs only 5 to 12 levels of 8-bit
colour across hundreds of pixels, so every level is a 40–100 px band.
The overlay film grain hides those steps in the drawn frames, but it was
re-seeded 24 times a second. New noise on every frame is something x264
cannot predict from the previous frame, so at the reel's bitrate it
rounded the grain away and the bare steps came back as rings.

The tint comes from red, green and blue rounding to the next level at
slightly different radii. Video then stores those small colour
differences more coarsely than brightness. The rings move because the
glows' radius and strength are animated.

Ruled out by experiment on lossless frames: the JPEG frame capture, the
colour-range conversion, and x264's deblocking.

**Fix.** The grain is now still: the same pattern on every frame.
`fx.grain` reads the `STAGE_FX.grain.fps` setting, which existed but was
unused, and that setting is now 0. The encoder carries a still pattern
from frame to frame almost for free, so it survives the encode and keeps
dithering the steps. The encoder settings are unchanged.

Measured on 60 fps drafts of the three worst sections (dark 8×8 luma
blocks, sampled every half second):

| Section | Perfectly flat dark blocks | Mean run of identical luma |
Video bitrate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| End card | 83.8% → 26.4% | 19.1 → 3.4 px | 256 → 365 kb/s |
| Open | 83.2% → 32.7% | 25.1 → 3.9 px | 621 → 687 kb/s |
| Morph | 78.8% → 43.8% | 21.3 → 7.1 px | 718 → 758 kb/s |

The lossless frames measure about 1.6 px. A full-reel 60 fps measurement
of the same change put the shipped `showreel.mp4` at 35.1 → 38.5 MB
(+14% video bitrate). The 30 fps reel grew 4%.

**Look.** The grain no longer flickers. Over the end card's final hold,
only the rising motes move now. `ART.md`, `STORYBOARD.md` and the end
card's comments are updated to match.

Not done here: drawing the glows as native canvas gradients, which
Chromium dithers and the current scaled sprite does not, would further
reduce the faint colour fringing. It makes no difference after the
encode on its own.

`aube run typecheck:showreel` passes; `aube run test:showreel`: 166
pass, 1 skipped (needs a capture run not on this machine).

tagline, the install command, mise.jdx.dev and the glint arrive on an
eighth-beat grid. They take the same times, rounded, that the vocal used
to set. A few light effects mark the name, the URL and the glint.
- **Pitched effects follow the new track's chords** (F minor, C minor,
B♭, and F with no third where the track leans major). The old key change
on `cd ../dashboard` is gone.

reel is -17.0 LUFS integrated with a true peak of -2.8 dBTP before the
AAC encode. That is the target the old mix had. By act:

| Act | Loudness |
| --- | --- |
| Acts I–VI | -17.6 to -15.8 LUFS |
| Environments | -20 LUFS |
| Quiet stretch before the clone | -23 LUFS |
| Breath | -35 LUFS |
| Climax | -13.9 LUFS |

## How it's built

- **The bed.** `score/bed.opus` is the track, already arranged on reel
time: 436.000 s of 48 kHz stereo Ogg Opus, 11.5 MB, pinned by sha256 in
`score/bed.ts`. Suno rendered it at an exact 120 BPM, so it is trimmed
to its first downbeat and not stretched: every 2 s bar of the bed lines
up with two of the reel's 60 BPM beats. `score/BED.md` records where it
came from, how it was arranged, the measurements, and who owns it.
- **Playback.** The renderer reads the bed, checks its hash and format,
and passes it to the headless page in chunks of 20 MiB or less. The page
decodes it with `decodeAudioData`. `audio.ts` plays it on the music bus,
starting on an exact frame, so a draft rendered from the middle of the
reel plays the same samples as a full render. The bus keeps the ducking,
the section fader and the master limiter. A cross-correlation of the
full render against the decoded bed finds it at lag 0.
- **Removed.**
- The synthesized band: every section's drums, bass, lead and pads
layers, plus `band.ts` and the instruments only the band used.
- The end-card recording: `song.ts`, `mise-en-place.mp3`, and the ffmpeg
splice in the renderer.
  - The held B♭ minor handoff into the recording.
- **New task `mise run docs:showreel-bed`.** It fits a downloaded track
to the reel for next time. In order, it:
  1. Analyses the tempo, downbeat, key and chords.
2. Stretches the track onto the 2 s grid with a Rubber Band time map, or
skips this when the track is already on the grid, as this one is.
3. Arranges source bars onto reel bars from
`docs/.vitepress/showreel-bed/bed.toml`.
  4. Sets the level.
  5. Encodes Opus reproducibly.
6. Verifies the length, the ending, and the bar lines against the grid.
This track: median deviation 1 ms, 90th percentile 3 ms.

It needs ffmpeg, the Rubber Band CLI and uv, and is not part of the
render.

The render cache key already hashes everything under `theme/showreel`,
so the trusted docs deploy renders the new reel on merge. The PR draft
renders 129–131 s with the bed.

- `aube run typecheck:showreel` passes. `aube run test:showreel` runs
167 tests: 166 pass and 1 is skipped (it needs a capture run that isn't
on this machine). The new `test/bed.test.ts` checks:
- the file: its hash, the Ogg/Opus stream, and an exact 20,928,000-frame
length
  - routing: the bed reaches the music bus and never the reverb
- timing: frame-exact starts and offsets for mid-reel renders, and duck
scaling

that the end card's sounds land on its cues, and that switch's runs
follow the bed's chords.

rendered locally in 190 s, and its audio lines up with the audio-only
render.

ci: build real Windows releases on a dedicated release runner (#13899)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/387
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Real Windows x64 releases can now be built on a dedicated release runner
and account instead of the shared CI runner, so the binary that gets
signed is not built on a machine where pull-request code has run.
Nothing changes until a new repository variable is set.

## Why

`build-tarball-windows` is the job that produces the shipped `mise.exe`.
It uses no secrets itself (signing happens afterwards in the `release`
job on a hosted runner), so the risk this closes is build integrity: on
the shared runner, a pull-request job from a trusted author shares an
account, a Rust toolchain, compiler proxies and a build cache with
whatever builds the release.

## What changes

- **Routing.** The release PR's dry run keeps using the shared trusted
runner (`WINDOWS_SELF_HOSTED=true`). A real release uses `[self-hosted,
jdx-win-release-v1]` when the new repository variable
`WINDOWS_RELEASE_SELF_HOSTED` is `true` and the run starts from a `v*`
tag (push or dispatch) or from `main`, `release` or `mise`, the refs
that runner accepts. A dispatch from any other branch builds on the
hosted runner instead of failing on the runner's own refusal. Either
variable unset falls back to `windows-latest`, so a release never queues
for a machine that is off, and the new variable ships off.
- **No release build uses the mbx cache.** This removes the
`MBX_DISABLE` plumbing and the `mbx` switch from the release workflow
and `scripts/build-tarball.ps1` that came in with the runner PR. The dry
run rehearses the real build, so both use plain cargo from a clean
build, as the Linux and macOS release jobs do. The fat-LTO link of
`mise`, which is most of the time, was never cacheable.
- **Real releases never use the shared runner.** With only
`WINDOWS_SELF_HOSTED` set, a tag push builds on the hosted runner, not
the shared one.

## The runner side (not in this diff)

- A separate local account that cannot log in interactively, over RDP or
over the network, with its own Rust toolchain, temp directory and runner
directory. The shared runner's account has no access to any of them, and
the release account cannot write the shared runner's.
- The runner's binaries and configuration are read-only to its account
(only its work and log folders are writable), and runner self-update is
off, so a build step cannot rewrite the runner or its hook.
- A host-side job-started hook, set as a per-service environment value
the account cannot change, accepts only `release.yml` for `jdx/mise`,
started by `jdx` or `mise-en-dev`, on a `v*` tag push or a dispatch from
a `v*` tag, `main`, `release` or `mise`. It refuses pull requests,
schedules and everything else.
- The shared runners now also refuse real releases, so a routing mistake
cannot ship a release from the shared account.

## Verification

- The routing expression, checked against these trigger scenarios (dry
run, fork and untrusted PRs, tag push, dispatch from protected and
unprotected refs, each variable on and off, arm64): all route as
described above.
- Both hooks, invoked the way the runner invokes them in Windows
PowerShell and PowerShell 7: 17 release-hook cases and 6 shared-hook
cases, including outsiders, re-runs by an outsider, other repositories
and workflows, pull requests, branches, lookalike tags and mismatched
refs.
- Per-service environment overrides confirmed on a throwaway service;
directory permissions checked from the ACLs.
- Not exercised end to end: a real release has not run on the new
runner. The first one will build with fat LTO (about 26.5 minutes and 23
GB of memory when I measured it by hand on this machine).

To enable: `gh variable set WINDOWS_RELEASE_SELF_HOSTED --body true`. To
roll back: unset it.

ci: run trusted Windows jobs on a self-hosted runner (#13888)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/382
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Trusted Windows CI can now run on a dedicated machine with a 16-core
Ryzen 9 9950X and 64 GB of RAM, instead of 4-vCPU `windows-latest`
runners. Untrusted runs and arm64 builds are unchanged.

## What changes

- **Runner selection.** For trusted runs (the same `jdx` / `mise-en-dev`
rule `test.yml` already uses), `build-windows`, `windows-unit`,
`windows-lint` and the x64 `build-tarball-windows` job target
`[self-hosted, jdx-win-trusted-v1]`. Everything else keeps
`windows-latest` / `windows-11-arm`. `windows-e2e` deliberately stays on
`windows-latest`: on the runner, 13 of ~310 tests failed because they
need an interactive desktop, Task Scheduler or a user-level logon that a
runner service cannot provide (console-window and scheduled-task tests),
and the suite is not compile-bound, so there was little to gain.
- **Kill switch.** Jobs only use the machine while the repository
variable `WINDOWS_SELF_HOSTED` is `true`. Unset (the default), every
Windows job runs on hosted runners exactly as today, so merging this is
safe while the machine is offline, and flipping the variable off is the
one-step fallback.
- **Shared build cache.** Trusted build, test and lint jobs call `mbx
build|test|clippy` against one shared local store on the machine. This
needs mbx 1.21.1, which caches Windows proc-macros and build scripts
linked with `-C link-arg=/STACK:...` (mr-boxington#619); `mise.lock`
pins that version.
- **Release rule.** Only the release PR's dry run may use the cache. A
real release (tag push or manual dispatch) sets `MBX_DISABLE=1` and
always compiles from scratch with plain cargo, so a bad cache entry can
never reach a shipped artifact. `scripts/build-tarball.ps1` only
switches to `mbx` when `MBX_DISABLE=0` and `mbx` exists.
- **Fat LTO on Windows x64 releases.** `scripts/build-tarball.ps1`
forced thin LTO because the hosted runner could not finish a fat link
inside the job timeout. It now forces thin only on machines with under
48 GB of RAM, so the self-hosted runner builds with the `serious`
profile's default fat LTO like the other platforms. Hosted runners keep
thin.

## Why this is safe to run on a public repo

A repository-scoped runner can be selected by any workflow, including
one edited in a fork's pull request, so the machine does not rely on
workflow YAML. A host-side `ACTIONS_RUNNER_HOOK_JOB_STARTED` hook runs
before any step and refuses everything except: repository `jdx/mise`;
both the actor and the triggering actor being `jdx` or `mise-en-dev`;
protected refs (`main`, `release`, `mise`, `v*` tags) for push, dispatch
and schedule events; or a pull request from this repository with a
trusted author. It fails closed, runs as an unprivileged account that
cannot log in, and the runner account cannot modify the hook. I tested
the hook against simulated outsider fork PRs, a maintainer re-running or
pushing to an outsider's fork, a deleted fork head, a missing event
payload, other repositories, unlisted workflows, unprotected refs,
lookalike accounts, `pull_request_target` and `workflow_run`.

Not part of this PR: the repository's fork-PR approval setting is still
`first_time_contributors_new_to_github`; the hook makes that safe for
this runner, but tightening it is a separate decision.

## Measurements

Real whole-job times from this PR's CI on the self-hosted runners,
against one recent successful `main` run on `windows-latest`. Single
runs, so indicative:

| Job | Hosted (`windows-latest`) | Self-hosted |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `build-windows` | 577 s | 246 s |
| `windows-lint` (clippy) | 634 s | 169 s |
| `windows-unit` (`cargo test` + workspace members) | 624 s | 392 s |
| `windows-e2e` | 645 s | stays hosted (see above) |
| Windows x64 release build | thin LTO (fat ran 65+ min or hit the
timeout) | fat LTO, 26.5 min, 23 GB peak (measured on the machine) |

With mbx 1.21.1, rebuilding `build-windows`'s command from a deleted
`target` directory takes about 47 s (1229 cache hits, 0 misses), against
232 s for plain cargo on the same machine. Earlier mbx versions missed
about 175 compilations on every Windows rebuild and gained nothing. The
self-hosted jobs also skip `Swatinem/rust-cache`, since the machine
keeps its Cargo state and the mbx store between jobs, and the cache can
be dropped without touching anything else.

## Test plan

- [x] zizmor reports no new findings on the changed workflows.
- [x] `build-windows`, `windows-unit` and `windows-lint` pass on the
self-hosted runners in this PR's CI, with the trust hook accepting the
pull-request jobs.
- [x] Ran the Windows e2e suite on the runner service: 287 passed, 13
failed (desktop/scheduler/logon-dependent), which is why e2e stays
hosted.
- [ ] A release dry run and a tag release after merge.

Follow-ups, deliberately not here: a separate runner and account for
release signing, and moving arm64 off hosted runners.

fix(daemons): render env and vars in daemon commands at launch (#13894)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/385
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Fixes #13891.

A daemon command that referenced mise's `[env]` or `[vars]` failed to
start:

```toml
[vars]
test_var = "test_var_value"

[daemons.test-var]
run = "exec echo '{{ vars.test_var }}'"
```

```
pitchfork ERROR Template render error ...: Variable `vars` is not defined. Available variables: daemons, dir, host, id, name, ...
```

Pitchfork renders `run` before it launches the `mise x` wrapper, so it
never sees mise's config. Mise now finishes the job at launch. When
pitchfork passes a command through unrendered, `mise x` renders it with
the project's `[env]`, `[vars]` and all of mise's template filters (such
as `quote`), plus pitchfork's own variables:

```toml
[env]
GREETING_SUFFIX = "!"

[vars]
greeting = "it's"

[daemons.hello]
run = "exec echo {{ vars.greeting | quote }}{{ env.GREETING_SUFFIX }} from {{ name }}"
```

The daemon prints `it's! from hello`, and `{{ name }}` still comes from
pitchfork.

Why this shape: mise `[env]` can hold decrypted secrets, so it is never
copied into the generated pitchfork file, and mise does not scan the
template text to decide which tags are its own. Rendering happens in the
daemon's own directory, so it uses that project's vars, including for a
daemon a parent project declares.

Requirements and limits:
- Needs the pitchfork change in jdx/pitchfork#966, so a pitchfork
release newer than 2.29.0. With an older pitchfork the failure above
remains.
- Applies to `run` only; `env`, hooks and the ready/health fields still
use pitchfork's variables.
- `mise x` reads the context from `PITCHFORK_TEMPLATE_CONTEXT` (JSON),
removes it from the command's environment, and only renders when it is
set; `mise x` called elsewhere is unchanged.

Tests: new e2e `test_exec_pitchfork_template_context` covers
env/vars/pitchfork variables, the variable not leaking to child
processes, and render errors. I also ran the issue's reproduction
against a local build of the pitchfork PR end to end (`test_env_value
test_var_value t`). The daemons unit tests and clippy pass. Docs updated
in `docs/daemons.md`.

fix(brew-cask): stop reinstalling pkg casks whose uninstall ids span architectures (#13893)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/384
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise bootstrap packages install` reinstalled pkg-based `brew-cask`
packages such as `google-drive` on every run, even though they were
installed and had a current mise receipt. `--dry-run` always planned
`install cask google-drive/...`.

**Cause.** The receipt recorded every id from the cask's `uninstall
pkgutil` list, and the installed check required all of them to be
registered. Homebrew treats that list as "ids to remove if present", so
it can include other architectures or optional components. For
google-drive on Apple silicon, only `com.google.drivefs.arm64` and
`com.google.drivefs.shortcuts` register, so the `x86_64` and FUSE ids
made the cask report missing forever.

**Fix.** When the receipt is written, each declared pattern is resolved
with `pkgutil --pkgs=<pattern>` and only the patterns that matched an
installed receipt are stored (the patterns, not the expanded ids, so a
self-updating package that replaces a receipt with a newer matching id
is still found). The all-must-exist check is unchanged, but now runs
against patterns that can match on this machine. If no pattern matches,
the declared list is kept so an unverifiable install is still reported
missing.

Receipts written by earlier versions keep the full list, so an affected
cask is reinstalled once on the next `mise bootstrap packages install`,
which writes a corrected receipt.

Validated with new unit tests (google-drive id set, wildcard pattern
retention, no-match fallback, receipt round-trip) and the existing cask
tests. Not exercised against a real pkg install.

Fixes #13890

fix(release): back up alpine bump to GitHub and allow SSH push to GitLab (#13892)

The `release-alpine` job for v2026.10.0 spent 38 minutes building the
apks, then failed on `git push` to `gitlab.alpinelinux.org` with an HTTP
418. Alpine's `go-away` bot-challenge proxy blocks git-over-HTTPS from
CI IP ranges, so the Alpine package bump (and its GitLab MR) never went
out. The same thing failed v2026.8.0, v2026.8.10, v2026.9.0 and
v2026.9.10; [#13286](https://github.com/jdx/mise/pull/13286) worked
around the clone but not the push.

This makes the push avoid the challenge, and makes a failure cheap to
recover from:

- **SSH push.** When the `ALPINE_GITLAB_SSH_KEY` secret is set, the
script pushes to `jdxcode/aports` over SSH with a pinned ed25519 host
key. The proxy only fronts HTTP; sshd is separate. Without the secret,
behavior is unchanged (HTTPS with the token).
- **GitHub backup.** Before pushing to GitLab, the bump is pushed to
`mise-<version>` on `github.com/jdx/aports` (a fork of
`alpinelinux/aports`). Best effort: a failure only warns.
- **Retries.** The GitLab push is tried 3 times (1 and 2 minute
backoff), since the block has come and gone before.
- **Recovery output.** If all attempts fail, the job errors with the
exact commands to finish by hand from the GitHub branch (clone, create
local `mise` branch, push to GitLab over SSH, `glab mr create`), or says
to re-run if the backup push failed too. No more 40 minute rebuild.
- Credentials (SSH key write, token-bearing backup remote) are kept out
of `set -x` output.

## Setup already done
- `jdx/aports` fork exists; `mise-en-dev` has write access, and the
workflow's `MISE_GH_TOKEN` is used for the backup push.
- A write deploy key is registered on `jdxcode/aports` and its private
half is stored as `ALPINE_GITLAB_SSH_KEY` in this repo. Verified from a
laptop: `git ls-remote` and the receive-pack advertisement succeed with
it, and the host key matches the pinned one.

## Not verified
- SSH from GitHub's runner IPs, and `glab mr create` (HTTPS API with the
token) from CI, haven't run since the 418. Needs a `workflow_dispatch`
with `dry_run=false` after merge, then a re-run for v2026.10.0.

https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/380

A Packslip install can successfully extract its executable yet fail to
fetch a declared skill, for example when GitHub's contents API is
temporarily unavailable. mise previously reported that install as
complete and skipped it on a later plain `mise install`.

This keeps the usable binary in place but leaves the install incomplete
and returns an error when a fetch-enabled declared skill remains
unavailable after all applicable sources have been tried. A later plain
`mise install` repairs just the missing declared skills in place.
Shipped skills, successful fallback sources, `skills.fetch = false`,
exec-only skills with `packslip.exec = false`, unrelated optional
resources, and integrity failures retain their existing behavior.

The regression coverage exercises failed staging cleanup, fallback
satisfaction, and intentionally disabled skill sources.

locally because the approved disposable VM could not receive the
checkout through its network policy; CI is pending.

reinstall is required). Nested **`mise`** calls from postinstall keep

deadlock on locks.

as required vs intentionally skipped (**`skills.fetch`**, exec-only with
**`packslip.exec` off**), plus regression tests for retry lifecycle,
partial skill staging, and fallback satisfaction.

commits.message:
fix: keep SD-font kerning and ligatures in edge cases (#3838)

## Summary

* **What is the goal of this PR?**
Fix five bugs in `SdCardFont`'s per-page kern matrix and ligatures. Each
has a host test that fails on develop. This is bugfixes separated from
PR #3831 to keep PR small and reviewable.

* **What changes are included?** One commit in
`lib/EpdFont/SdCardFont.{h,cpp}`:

1. **Kerning lost after a request is served from glyphs cached without
kerning.** A kern-wanting prewarm whose
glyphs are all cached by a kern-free prewarm (UI strings) tops up the
kern matrix without re-reading glyphs. It
built the matrix for the request only, and decided whether to build from
`miniKernLeftClassCount == 0`. Once a
top-up found pairs, later requests whose pairs it missed skipped the
build and drew unkerned. Example: cache
`ABCDEF` without kerning, then request `AB` and then `CD`; `C`–`D`
returns 0 instead of −5.
- The top-up now covers every cached glyph, and a `miniKernBuilt` flag
records that coverage. A full rebuild
sets it from its own kern build, and freeing the mini kern clears it.
- If the cached-glyph list cannot be allocated, the top-up covers the
request only, logs the failure, and leaves
       the flag unset so the next request builds again.
2. **Class IDs past the matrix read outside the row buffer.** A class ID
above the font's class count indexed past
the `kernRightClassCount`-byte row buffer (heap read past the allocation
under ASan) and seeked to a row past
the matrix. Such entries are now treated as unkerned when the class
tables load. Fonts are user-supplied files.
3. **The matrix loops never ended with 255 classes.**
`numLeft`/`numRight` and the loop counters were `uint8_t`, so
`newL <= numLeft` stayed true when a page used all 255 classes. The
counters are now `uint16_t`.
4. **A failed mini kern build dropped the page's ligatures.** The kern
and ligature pointers were applied together
only when the build succeeded. They are now applied whenever the tables
loaded; a failed build leaves the mini
     kern empty, so the page keeps its ligatures and kerns as none.
5. **Fonts without kern classes lost ligatures on the same cached-glyph
path.** The top-up in (1) is also what
attaches the ligature table, and it only ran when the font had kern
classes. A font with ligatures but no kern
classes drew those requests without ligatures. It now runs for every
font; without kern classes the matrix build
     returns at once and reads nothing.

Normal page prewarms are unchanged: a full rebuild still builds the
matrix for the page's codepoints, and the
  number of mini kern builds per boot is the same.

## Scope Check

- [x] I have read SCOPE.md and ROADMAP.md.
- [x] This PR is **not** a new built-in theme.
- [x] This PR is **not** a new external network connector.
- [x] This PR is **not** an interactive app, writing tool,
RSS/news/browser, media playback, or PDF feature.
- [x] The stock firmware does not already handle this well, **and** no
other popular CrossPoint fork already does.
      (Not audited; this is a bug fix in the SD-font cache.)
- [x] If this PR touches `freeink-sdk/`, `lib/hal/`, the bootloader,
OTA, or recovery code, I have coordinated with
      the relevant maintainer. (It touches none of them.)

#3831 builds on this PR and carries the same fixes into its rewrite of
the kern path.

## Additional Context

### Tests

`SdCardFontTest` gains a small kerning fixture (six Latin glyphs,
configurable class tables, an optional ligature)
and seven cases. On develop:

| Test | develop | This PR |
|---|---|---|
| `KernRequestsServedFromAKernFreeMiniStillKern` (bug 1) | fails:
`C`–`D` returns 0 | passes |
| `ClassIdsPastTheMatrixAreUnkerned` (bug 2) | ASan heap-buffer-overflow
in `buildMiniKernMatrix` | passes |
| `PagesCanUseAll255KernClasses` (bug 3) | aborts (UBSan, the loop
wraps) | passes |
| `AFailedKernBuildKeepsTheLigatures` (bug 4) | fails: no ligature |
passes |
| `LigatureRequestsServedFromAKernFreeMiniGetLigatures` (bug 5) | fails:
no ligature | passes |
| `PagesKernWithTheFontsClassMatrix`,
`RedrawsAfterAKernFreeRebuildStillKern` | pass | pass |

The last two guard the normal path and the new flag after a kern-free
rebuild.

### Device check

X3, `develop` `813aaa12` vs this PR, both with identical #3510
serial-control instrumentation, `default` env
(LOG_LEVEL=2), Pretendard 16. Three interleaved cold pairs per book,
same protocol as #3831 (cold open, 6 + 6 page
turns, 40 turns of background layout, chapter restore, Home).

| | Korean: develop | PR | Change | English: develop | PR | Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Total page render (median) | 1,279.5 ms | 1,278.5 ms | −0.5 ms
(matched) | 1,146.5 ms | 1,144 ms | −0.5 ms (matched) |
| Font preparation (`prewarm`) | 117 ms | 116.5 ms | −0.5 ms | 32 ms |
32 ms | 0 |
| Mini kern builds per boot | 57 | 57 | 0 | 68 | 68 | 0 |
| Since-boot Min Free | 19,688 B | 19,688 B | 0 | 31,276 B | 31,276 B |
0 |
| Largest block in layout samples: min / median | 15,348 / 34,804 B |
15,348 / 34,804 B | 0 / 0 | 49,140 / 57,332 B | 49,140 / 57,332 B | 0 /
0 |
| Post-page sample: free / largest block | 71,640 / 59,380 B | 71,640 /
59,380 B | 0 / 0 | 74,016 / 61,428 B | 74,016 / 61,428 B | 0 / 0 |
| Home after exit: free / largest block | 111,740 / 98,292 B | 111,740 /
98,292 B | 0 / 0 | 112,680 / 65,524 B | 112,680 / 65,524 B | 0 / 0 |

All page landings match, and all 18 paired captures are identical in the
reading area (the full-frame differences
are in the battery footer). The fixed paths do not run in this workload,
so heap and timing are unchanged. These
runs used the commit before fix 5 was added; Pretendard has kern
classes, so fix 5 does not change its path.

* Memory / flash impact: static RAM unchanged. Flash +294 B (plain
`default` builds). The cached-glyph list is a
temporary allocation of up to 2 KB (`miniGlyphCount` × 4 B, at most 512
glyphs) during a kern top-up only.

### Verification

- `pio run -e default` passes. Formatted with `./bin/clang-format-fix
-g`.
- Host tests: 431/431 pass. The SD-font tests also pass under
ASan/UBSan.

Did you use AI tools to help write this code? _**YES**_ — AI tools
assisted with the code review that found these
bugs, the fixes, testing, and this description.

refactor(relay): bind HTTP tenants through one shadow-aware helper (#8062)

Adds `bind_tenant()`, a single helper that resolves the community from
the request `Host` and records the NIP-FI shadow verdict when binding
fails. Ten protected HTTP handlers previously duplicated the Host lookup
and called `observe_unbound` in their own failure branches, so each one
had to remember the observer call. Moving those ten handlers onto the
helper makes recording the verdict part of binding itself, and
`observe_unbound` becomes private to the shadow module. Each caller
keeps its existing rejection response, so Off/Enforce behavior is
unchanged.

`bind_community()` stays directly callable. Routes exempt from NIP-FI
(invite claim, webhooks, NIP-05 and NIP-11 metadata) keep using it, and
the WebSocket and audio upgrades record their own verdicts before they
bind. A new protected HTTP handler should bind through `bind_tenant()`.

🤖 Authored by Duncan (agent) on behalf of Will.

Signed-off-by: Will Pfleger <pfleger.will@gmail.com>
Co-authored-by: Duncan <dcfd242e557282d7a1e2cf2e6877522682f1e5c6156dc92ca7d90eaedd3b0f95@buzz.block.builderlab.xyz>

feat(relay): add NIP-FI shadow mode for HTTP, WebSocket and admin (#8034)

Stack: this PR → #8062

🤖 Follows #8028 (merged).

Adds `BUZZ_NIP_FI_MODE=shadow`. The relay loads and validates the full
enforce configuration (issuers, communities, lifetimes, command
issuers), evaluates NIP-FI evidence wherever enforce would decide, and
records what enforce would have done, while every request, upgrade and
session behaves exactly as in `off`. The one approved exception is admin
disconnect: shadow verifies the command and returns `200`, where Off has
no verifier and returns `503`. It lets an operator measure the
would-deny rate, including Hosts missing from `BUZZ_NIP_FI_COMMUNITIES`,
before switching to `enforce`.

- **Mode predicates.** `NipFiMode` gains `is_off`, `restricts`,
`evaluates`, `enforces`, `denies_unconditionally` and `observes_only`,
built on two exhaustive `match` bases (`restricts`, `evaluates`);
`is_off` is a `matches!` and the rest derive from the bases, so a new
mode cannot silently fall into one side. Every call site uses them,
including the Git membership-lookup failure from #8005, which uses
`restricts()` so shadow keeps Off's body. A test scans each crate's
`src/` and fails on any `NipFiMode::<variant>` in production code
outside the predicate definitions and the env parser, which catches
`==`, `matches!` on any number of lines, `if let` and or-patterns.
- **Startup.** Shadow goes through enforce's path, so every enforce
startup refusal applies, including the required connection lifetime.
Missing-setting errors name the configured mode through one formatter
(`mode_requires`); the enforce text is byte-identical. Shadow builds the
assertion verifier and claims command replays under its own Redis
prefix, both through the production `AppState::new`.
- **HTTP and Blossom.** `admit_nip_fi_http` keeps Off's result in shadow
and additionally replays enforce in enforce's order: first the router
guard's steps (community, then assertion), then the handler's steps
(NIP-98, pairing, deny set) on the same NIP-98 proof, through
`evaluate_enforce_steps`, which enforce shares. A Host mapped in config
but missing from the communities table, with a valid assertion, records
an admit, because enforce's guard passes and its 404 is not a NIP-FI
denial. A dev-mode `X-Pubkey` identity is marked unsigned and is never
an enforce proof, so shadow records it as a `nip98` would-deny. On
bridge and Blossom routes, the strict proof check (payload tag, Blossom
`Strict`) runs as a separate pure check that consumes no replay entry
and records on its own series, so it never counts as an admission
verdict. Shadow records exactly one verdict for every identity,
community or credential refusal enforce would make, with Off's status,
body and challenge unchanged: bridge, workflows, Blossom, Git transport
and settings, GIF search and share, and invite minting record the
`community` would-deny when the Host is unmapped. Git's missing or
malformed credentials still reject before any database work, and shadow
records the enforce verdict for that failed proof. The router guard
stays transparent in shadow.
- **WebSocket, root and audio.** The upgrade check evaluates the
attached assertion once. An upgrade enforce would refuse records that
would-deny; otherwise the assertion goes into a shadow-only session
object and the upgrade returns as in Off. The assertion never reaches
the connection, the identity registries, the admission gate, terminal
frames or cancellation. Each session records at most one admission
verdict. **Pairing** is recorded on both ingresses right after a valid
NIP-42 proof, before ordinary relay policy, where enforce pairs: a key
mismatch or claimless assertion is a `pairing` denial. **The deny-set
check** runs where enforce runs it, after registration: a hit is a
`deny_set` denial, and a clean read keeps the session pending and
registered. **The admit** is recorded only when the connection is
actually admitted: on root at the AUTH commit, after ordinary policy; on
audio when the participant join transaction commits, after relay
membership, channel membership, the final ban and membership decision,
mesh routing and the join's own checks, and before publication. A NIP-42
failure, which comes before pairing, and any refusal between pairing and
the admit (ordinary policy, mesh, or a join refusal inside the join
transaction) retires the observer when the refusal is decided, before
any refusal frame, rollback or cleanup is awaited, so it leaves no
record even if the deadline passes during that cleanup. A record-only
deadline task, armed at upgrade with enforce's
`compute_session_deadline`, records `expired` when enforce would have
closed an admitted session. If the deadline passes while the session is
still pending, that is its single admission verdict, a denial with
`stage=deadline`, and a later AUTH records nothing. A deny for the key
(admin or cross-pod) records `revoked` on an admitted session; if it
arrives after the deny-set check but before the admit, including a deny
refused for capacity, the session keeps a pending-revocation mark and
records the admit followed by exactly one `revoked` end, matching
enforce's phase-independent close, and the deadline cannot take that
end. The phase, the mark and retirement change together under one
session lock. Each session records at most one end. The session holds
the socket's cancellation token for recording only: once the socket is
cancelled, no transition records anything, even while connection
references remain (a cancel fence; the token never feeds a close
action). Upgrade would-denies carry the ingress route, `ws` or `audio`.
- **Admin disconnect.** Shadow verifies the command and records the deny
entry, so later admissions record would-denies, but closes no session;
the response stays `{"disconnected": true}`. Shadow publishes cross-pod
on its own channel, `buzz:nip-fi:shadow-disconnect`, which only shadow
pods subscribe to, so no enforce pod (including older builds that know
only `buzz:nip-fi:disconnect`) acts on a shadow command. Shadow pods
also keep listening on `buzz:nip-fi:disconnect`, so their deny record
includes enforce's real disconnects. Shadow claims command replays under
`buzz:nip-fi:shadow-command:{hash}`: replays are still rejected within
shadow, and a shadow accept never uses up the enforce claim. Enforce and
Off keep the same channel, keys and close behavior.
- **NIP-11.** Shadow serves the same document as enforce, including
`limitation.federated_identity`, because clients only attach evidence to
a relay that advertises it.

## Recording

| Series | Labels | One increment per |
|---|---|---|
| `buzz_nip_fi_shadow_total` | `route` (`http`, `ws`, `audio`), `stage`,
`outcome`, `community` | decision enforce would make: an HTTP admission,
a refused upgrade, a session's NIP-FI AUTH decision, or its deadline
passing before AUTH (`stage=deadline`) |
| `buzz_nip_fi_shadow_strict_proof_total` | `route` (`bridge`,
`blossom`), `outcome` (`pass`, `rejected`), `community` | strict NIP-98
side check |
| `buzz_nip_fi_shadow_session_end_total` | `route` (`ws`, `audio`),
`reason` (`expired`, `revoked`), `community` | admitted session enforce
would have ended (admitted sessions only) |
| `buzz_nip_fi_shadow_disconnect_total` | `route` (`admin`,
`cross_pod`), `outcome` | disconnect-path event, in place of the real
disconnect, lag, capacity and poison counters |

`community` is the configured canonical URI or `unmapped`, never the raw
`Host`; an unmapped or empty Host records `stage=community,
outcome=unavailable`. A shadow pod never moves an enforce disconnect or
failure counter. Strict-proof rates use their own `pass + rejected`
total, and session-end rates divide by the `admit` count for the same
route. There is no per-verdict `info` log; a would-deny writes a `debug`
line with no token, claim or issuer. The pre-existing enforce `debug`
line for the proven NIP-98 key is shared and also fires in shadow. Admin
commands rejected for a bad header, body or proof, a replay, or a
dependency error record no shadow verdict; only capacity rejection is
counted.

## Not observed

- Handler-side path-validation exits: an invalid Git owner or repo name
on default-branch, a media path that is not a valid hash, and a Git pack
URL with a query string record nothing from the handler. The router
guard still records what enforce would refuse at the guard (for example
a missing assertion), because enforce refuses those requests before it
validates the path.
- A refusal that is not a NIP-FI decision, such as a tenant-binding 404
behind a passing guard, or an ordinary WebSocket refusal after pairing
(a ban, membership or join refusal before admission).

## Follow-ups

- A bounded `route` label per HTTP surface (bridge, Blossom, Git, …) on
`buzz_nip_fi_shadow_total`; today every HTTP verdict carries
`route=http`.
- One shared helper for the ten copied `observe_unbound` recording
hooks, stacked on this PR.

The shadow recorder and session suites and the root pairing witness run
in `just test-unit` and the `scripts/run-tests.sh` fallback; the
`AppState::new` shadow witness, which exercises the command verifier
against real Redis, runs in the `external_infra_redis` lane. NIP-FI env
tests recover a poisoned env lock so one panic cannot cascade.

BUZZ-175: Add application-owned writer lock foundations (#7706)

## Summary

Buzz is moving database invariants from triggers and foreign keys into
application-owned transaction protocols. This PR adds the first
transition foundations while preserving all current database backstops.

- Add a shared community-write lock for single-community writer
transactions, and make deletion lifecycle transitions take the matching
exclusive lock. A supported serving transaction never spans communities.
- Add shared event-writer and exclusive replica-probe lock ordering
around the existing heartbeat publication model.
- Document the supported writer contract, reviewed backfill path, and
transition gates.
- Keep one replica-floor publication concept and remove an unrelated
reconciliation-script edit found during review. This narrows the change
rather than adding parallel protocols.

The blast radius is limited to new opt-in writer helpers plus lock
acquisition in deletion and replica probing. Existing trigger and GUC
enforcement remains authoritative, so callers can migrate in later pull
requests.

### Related issue

[BUZZ-175](https://linear.app/squareup/issue/BUZZ-175). This is the
first implementation slice from the OSC migration plan.

No manual testing. CI covers the Rust checks and database tests added
here.

fix(acp): steer running turns with edited mentions (#6132)

🤖
## Summary
Some agents can take a new message into a turn that is already running.
This is called "native steering." Before this PR, an edit that arrived
during a turn always cancelled the turn and started it again. Now the
edit is steered into the running turn, like any other new message. The
steered edit still points at the original message and its thread, so the
agent replies in the right place.

- The steer text carries the edit's route: `Edit of: …`, plus the
original's thread root.
- **Steer only within the same reply thread.** A native steer keeps the
running turn's `<context>`, so the reply goes where that `<context>`
points. The queue now records each running turn's reply thread. A
message is steered natively only when it replies in that same thread.
Under channel sessions one session spans threads, so an edit for another
thread (or another top-level message) takes the cancel-and-restart path.
Its re-prompt carries the message's own full `<context>`, with channel,
project, and profile data. The same rule applies to ordinary steered
messages, which had the same gap before this PR.
- **Per-thread sessions:** the edit steers only a turn running in the
same session as its original message. An edit in thread A is never added
to a turn running in thread B. If no turn is running in that session,
the edit waits in the queue as its own item.
- **Channel sessions** (the default): the channel has one session. A
running turn receives the edit natively only when the edit replies in
that turn's thread.
- If native steering is not available, or the transport fails or the
agent rejects the steer, the existing cancel-and-restart fallback runs.
If the agent returns another error, or the turn has already finished,
the edit goes back to the queue for normal delivery. In every case the
queued edit keeps its route.

## Details
- #4741 looks up the original message once, before the edit is queued.
This PR passes that stored route to the existing steer path, and uses
the same session the edit was queued under. No new lookup or preparation
step is needed.
- Removal, re-add, and fallback all use the existing lifecycle for
withheld steers.

### Stack
**3 of 3**. #6131 is merged; this PR is now based on `main`.

### Related issue
Part of #2540 (fixed by #6131). This PR adds the running-turn behavior.

### Testing
- `cargo test -p buzz-acp --all-targets` passes. The one test that fails
when the git setting `nostr.keyfile` is set is described in #4741.
- Tests check that the steer text carries the original's route, and that
the listener gives the steer path the same route and session it queues.
- End-to-end tests send a routed edit through the listener's steer
decision under channel sessions. An edit in the running turn's thread,
and an edit of the running top-level message, steer natively with no
cancel. An edit for thread B during a thread-A turn, and an edit of
another top-level message, send no native steer and take cancel+merge.
Removing the same-thread check makes both cross-thread tests fail.

fix(acp): wake quiet hosts for respawns and queued retries (#7459)

## Problem

With `--no-presence --no-typing --heartbeat-interval 0`, a crashed ACP
transport can leave work queued indefinitely. Background respawn results
were only drained before `select!`; neither their arrival nor queue
retry eligibility woke the host. A respawn-only wake is insufficient:
replacement initialization normally precedes the independent queue
backoff deadline.

## Change

- Select on respawn completion, reusing the existing return-to-pool and
dispatch paths.
- Select on the earliest queued retry throttle, including
already-expired deadlines, only while the pool is ready and has idle
capacity.
- Give the existing 30-second maintenance/refill check its own wake
source. Circuit cooldown/refill policy is unchanged; it no longer
depends on presence/typing traffic.
- Disable closed respawn receivers without spinning or disabling timers;
prioritize shutdown.
- Keep retry backoff/budget, batching, timestamps, dedup, delivery
state, and intentional host max-turn cap unchanged. Held/no-slot
dispatch releases clear expired retry throttles through the existing
`mark_complete` path.

No reconnect/gateway changes or adapter retry engine. Based directly on
main, independent of other ACP plumbing work. Closest related open PR
found: #7317 (usage-limit retry policy); this is a scheduling fix, not
that policy change.

## Validation

- `cargo test -p buzz-acp`: 920 library tests + 9 integration tests
pass.
- Five new Rust tests exercise the production wake helper and queue

Add kiln-conventions skill: shared code rules, area gotchas and a diff gate

Adds .agents/skills/kiln-conventions, which agents invoke before writing or
changing code and reviewers apply when reviewing:

- rules.md: the 23 universal rules (comments, startup and entry points, state
  and globals, config, modules and layering, library vs application, async I/O,
  grandfathering), each with a bad/good example and the gate rule id where one
  applies. It now holds the content of the AGENTS.md "Code Comments" section.
- conventions_gate.py (stdlib only) with 135 tests: checks the added lines of a
  --range or --worktree diff (untracked files included), or whole --files.
  Rules: history-comment, global-stmt, bool-env, env-access,
  core-config-shared, lib-imports-routes (FAIL); module-level-call,
  module-level-construct, module-level-subscribe (WARN). Kiln-specific
  settings live in gate_config.json and gate_allow.txt.
- references/core.md, server_desktop.md, web_ui.md: gotchas, where things go
  and startup for each area. Every symbol they name was checked against the
  current code. Nothing describes bugs that have open fix PRs.
- SKILL.md: the flow (rules, area refs, gate, self-check), the path table,
  the kiln-ui pointer, reporting rules for FAIL/WARN, and gate maintenance.
- Wiring: AGENTS.md invokes the skill and points its Code Comments section at
  rules.md section A; code_review_guidelines.md applies the rules and runs the
  gate, replacing the comment and globals bullets; kiln-ui links to
  references/web_ui.md.
- Spec project specs/projects/code_conventions (overview, functional spec,
  architecture, plan, phase 1 plan, audit) and the history-comment baseline
  (38 hits) that phase 3's comment sweep works from.

Calibration over libs/core/kiln_ai, libs/server/kiln_server, app/desktop and
app/web_ui/src: 61 core-config-shared, 38 history-comment, 18 env-access,
10 global-stmt, 4 lib-imports-routes FAIL; 13 module-level-call,
11 module-level-construct, 2 module-level-subscribe WARN; 4 allowlisted.
The whole tree takes about 1.4 s and a 30-commit range about 0.5 s.

Deviations from the spec:
- History phrases: the spec listed a starting set. The code tightens it from
  calibration (86 hits, about half false positives, down to 38 with about 3).
  "used to" matches only after we/it/they/this/that/which/who/never, because
  the spec's passive-word guard still hit "Used to filter" and "only used to".
  "no longer" skips runtime-state wording (matches, exists, available, ...)
  and "can/could no longer". "previously" skips "previously <word>ed".
  "changed from" needs the "changed from X to" form. "phase N" skips "Phase N:"
  step labels. "was removed" is dropped because its only hit was runtime
  wording.
- Globs: the spec said fnmatch. The code uses its own glob-to-regex where * and
  ? stay in one path segment and brackets are literal, because SvelteKit route
  folders are named [project_id].
- module-level-call: the spec's regex allowed a space before "(". The code
  needs "name(", because the spaced form matched prose in module docstrings.
- bool-env: the spec's regex also matched parse_bool(os.environ...). The code
  requires "bool(" to start a name.
- Config parsing also rejects unknown keys (exit 2), and main() takes a
  config_dir argument for tests that is not exposed on the CLI.
- gate_config.json: env_access_allowed also includes app/desktop/log_config.py,
  and skip_globs also skip specs/**, the e2e tests and the generated client.
  gate_allow.txt allows animation "PHASE N" comments and reading
  PATH/SHELL/HOME from os.environ.
- The spec said to replace a comment bullet under "General Agent Guidance" in
  AGENTS.md. The comment rules were a separate "Code Comments" section, so that
  section is collapsed to a one-line pointer instead.
- A gate FAIL that can't be fixed without an out-of-scope refactor (rules.md
  H23) is reported in the summary and PR with its rule id, path:line and the
  refactor it waits on, not allowlisted. The allowlist is only for hits that
  aren't violations.

commits.message:
macos: honor window-save-state=never for restorable windows (#14506)

With `window-save-state = never`, normal terminal windows are still
marked `isRestorable`. Ghostty disables saving through
`NSQuitAlwaysKeepsWindows`, but AppKit continued taking persistent-UI
window snapshots in my reproduction on macOS 27.2 (26B5091g).

Make `TerminalController.windowDidLoad()` also honor `never` when
setting `window.isRestorable`, and only assign the restoration class and
identifier when that flag is enabled. This adds no work to move, resize,
or rendering callbacks.

For newly created windows, `default` and `always` retain the existing
behavior, including the exclusion of windows launched with a custom
command. The follow-up commit also covers windows that are already open:
on config reload, each terminal window re-syncs its restoration state
through the same path used at window creation. Windows started with a
custom command stay excluded.

### Reproduction and measurements

I reproduced intermittent roughly 500 ms stalls while repeatedly
focusing left/right between several Ghostty windows and other
applications in OmniWM's Niri layout. `window-save-state = never` was
set before restarting Ghostty.

The issue reproduced on 1.3.1 and an unmodified build of `76895d97b`. In
the latter, paired process samples showed
`NSPersistentUIWindowSnapshotter` waiting through
`SLSConnectionSynchronizeSLSCATransaction`, alongside Ghostty's main
thread waiting on the connection lock under
`SLSConnectionSetLastSLSCATransaction`.

Comparing unmodified and patched builds of the same commit over two
approximately 20-second navigation captures:

| Measurement | Unmodified | Patched |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Focus presses | 113 | 129 |
| Successful Ghostty AX frame-write attempts | 2,155 | 2,995 |
| Ghostty AX frame-write attempts around 500 ms | 5 | 0 |
| Slowest Ghostty AX frame-write attempt | 539.8 ms | 22.5 ms |
| Ghostty main-thread samples in the CA/SkyLight connection-lock wait |
2,205 / 12,544 | 0 / 12,173 |

The persistent-UI snapshot worker was absent from the patched sample,
and navigation feels noticeably smoother. These are aggregate samples
from one before/after pair with different input counts, not a controlled
end-to-end latency benchmark. Both Ghostty builds used ReleaseLocal with
the same ReleaseFast core, while OmniWM remained the same instrumented
Debug process.

### Validation

- `macos/build.nu --action test`: 275 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
- New `macos/Tests/Terminal/TerminalControllerRestorationTests.swift`:
reload flips restoration on an open window between `never`, `default`
and `always`; custom-command windows stay non-restorable across reloads;
surface-level config changes leave it alone.
- `macos/build.nu --configuration ReleaseLocal`: passed.
- Strict SwiftLint on both changed files: passed.
- Manual navigation reproduction with the patched build: noticeably
smoother, with the results above.

### AI disclosure

I used OpenAI Codex to assist with diagnosis, implement the two-line
change, run verification, analyze the captures, and draft this
description. I reproduced the issue and tested the patched app
interactively.

macos: simplify window restoration setup

Let isRestorable control preservation while assigning the restoration
class and identifier consistently for every terminal window.

Remove the restoration test fixture that creates AppKit windows and
broadcasts configuration changes through the shared test host.

macos: update window restoration on config reload

Existing terminal windows retained their creation-time restoration
policy after configuration changes.

Refresh that policy on global config reload and share setup with window
creation, preserving the custom-command exclusion.
